papers.title: Gynecologic complications of disease-modifying therapy in women with multiple sclerosis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The long-term implications of multiple sclerosis (MS) disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) on gynecologic health remain understudied. We leverage a multicenter database to evaluate whether DMTs are associated with such complications. METHODS: We propensity-score 1:1 matched women with MS on (1) any versus no or (2) moderate- to high- (vs low-) immunosuppressive DMT by age, marital status, race, ethnicity, tobacco use, body mass index, human papilloma virus (HPV) vaccination, and gynecologic examinations/screenings. We then compared matched cohorts with risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: After matching, we analyzed 115,522 women with MS. The DMT (vs no DMT) group had increased risks of HPV positivity (RR: 1.52, 95% CI: 1.35-172), cervical dysplasia (RR: 1.40, 95% CI: 1.31-1.49), cervical cancer (RR: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.03-1.46), cervicitis (RR: 1.25, 95% CI: 1.10-1.41), herpes simplex virus positivity (RR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.14-1.45), vulvovaginitis (RR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.23-1.37), and Bartholin cysts/abscesses (RR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.07-1.76). Moderate- to high- (vs low-) immunosuppressive. DISCUSSION: MS DMTs, especially more immunosuppressive ones, are associated with increased risks of several gynecologic complications. Clinicians should recognize these potential sequelae of DMTs and integrate gynecological counseling/screening into MS care.

papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The long-term implications of multiple sclerosis (MS) disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) on gynecologic health remain understudied. We leverage a multicenter database to evaluate whether DMTs are associated with such complications. METHODS: We propensity-score 1:1 matched women with MS on (1) any versus no or (2) moderate- to high- (vs low-) immunosuppressive DMT by age, marital status, race, ethnicity, tobacco use, body mass index, human papilloma virus (HPV) vaccination, and gynecologic examinations/screenings. We then compared matched cohorts with risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: After matching, we analyzed 115,522 women with MS. The DMT (vs no DMT) group had increased risks of HPV positivity (RR: 1.52, 95% CI: 1.35-172), cervical dysplasia (RR: 1.40, 95% CI: 1.31-1.49), cervical cancer (RR: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.03-1.46), cervicitis (RR: 1.25, 95% CI: 1.10-1.41), herpes simplex virus positivity (RR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.14-1.45), vulvovaginitis (RR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.23-1.37), and Bartholin cysts/abscesses (RR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.07-1.76). Moderate- to high- (vs low-) immunosuppressive. DISCUSSION: MS DMTs, especially more immunosuppressive ones, are associated with increased risks of several gynecologic complications. Clinicians should recognize these potential sequelae of DMTs and integrate gynecological counseling/screening into MS care.

papers.title: РОЛЬ ВАГИНАЛЬНОГО МИКРОБИОМА В ПЕРСИСТЕНЦИИ ВИРУСА ПАПИЛЛОМЫ ЧЕЛОВЕКА И ПРОГРЕССИИ ЦЕРВИКАЛЬНОЙ ИНТРАЭПИТЕЛИАЛЬНОЙ НЕОПЛАЗИИ В РАК ШЕЙКИ МАТКИ
papers.abstract: В обзоре представлен анализ современных данных о взаимосвязи состава вагинального микробиома с течением папилломавирусной инфекции у женщин в Республике Беларусь. Приведены данные о молекулярно-эпидемиологических особенностях циркуляции вируса папилломы человека в белорусской популяции и перспективах использования пробиотических штаммов (Lactobacillus crispatus) в национальных клинических протоколах. The review presents an analysis of current data on the relationship between the composition of the vaginal microbiome and the course of human papillomavirus infection in women in the Republic of Belarus. Special attention is paid to the species diversity of lactobacilli and their role in the clearance or persistence of high-risk human papillomavirus. The mechanisms of progression of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia to cervical cancer against the background of dysbiotic disorders are considered. Data on the molecular and epidemiological features of human papillomavirus circulation in the Belarusian population and the prospects for using probiotic strains (Lactobacillus crispatus) in national clinical protocols are presented.

elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述综合了白俄罗斯人群中 HPV 分子流行病学特征的最新数据,并评估了益生菌菌株(特别是卷曲乳杆菌)在国家临床方案中的作用。它整合了乳酸杆菌的物种多样性及其与 高危型HPV 清除或持久性的关联,以及生态失调背景下宫颈上皮内瘤变进展为癌症的机制。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述的结论是,乳杆菌物种多样性,特别是卷曲乳杆菌,与 高危型HPV 的清除或持久性相关。它强调了宫颈上皮内瘤变进展为 宫颈癌 与阴道菌群失调状态有关,强调了益生菌干预在国家临床方案中的潜在作用。

papers.title: Trends in vaccination in pharmacy and medical settings among Medicaid recipients in the United States, 2018-2023: a claims analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Medicaid beneficiaries typically have low vaccination rates, in part due to limited access. Pharmacies provide easy-to-access locations for vaccination. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: This was a retrospective analysis of trends in pharmacy-based vaccination by age and race or ethnicity among Medicaid recipients aged ≥9 from 1 January 2018 (before the COVID-19 pandemic) to 31 December 2023. The percentage of all vaccinations administered at pharmacies and the overall percentage change in vaccination rates were determined. RESULTS: With some exceptions, overall routine and seasonal vaccination rates remained lower in 2023 than in 2018-2019. This was observed for human papillomavirus (HPV), influenza, and tetanus-containing (Tdap/Td) vaccines in adolescents and for hepatitis A, influenza, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and Tdap/Td vaccines in various adult age groups. The percentage of routine and seasonal vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased over the study period among adults, with increases of 5.2-17.5 percentage points for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, HPV, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and tetanus-containing vaccines among those aged 19-49. Across age groups, pharmacy-based vaccination was most frequent in White enrollees, followed by Black and then Hispanic enrollees, with smaller differentials in adults aged ≥65. CONCLUSIONS: Generally overall vaccine administration rates declined in Medicaid beneficiaries; however, the proportion administered at pharmacies increased.

papers.title_original: Trends in vaccination in pharmacy and medical settings among Medicaid recipients in the United States, 2018-2023: a claims analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Medicaid beneficiaries often face barriers to vaccination, including limited access, which contributes to low vaccination rates. The study aimed to assess whether pharmacy-based vaccination settings could mitigate these barriers and improve vaccination trends among this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a retrospective analysis of trends in pharmacy-based vaccination among Medicaid recipients aged 9 years or older from 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2023. The study evaluated the percentage of vaccinations administered at pharmacies and overall vaccination rates over time.
analysis.methods: The study determined the percentage of all vaccinations administered at pharmacies and calculated the overall percentage change in vaccination rates. It analyzed trends by age and race or ethnicity, focusing on routine and seasonal vaccines.
analysis.main_results: Overall routine and seasonal vaccination rates remained lower in 2023 than in 2018-2019 for most vaccines, including HPV, influenza, and Tdap/Td in adolescents, and hepatitis A, influenza, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and Tdap/Td in adults. The percentage of vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased among adults, with gains of 5.2-17.5 percentage points for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, HPV, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and tetanus-containing vaccines in those aged 19-49.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that while overall vaccination rates declined among Medicaid beneficiaries, the proportion of vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased, suggesting improved access through pharmacy settings. This trend was most pronounced in White enrollees, with smaller differentials in adults aged 65 and older.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that expanding pharmacy-based vaccination services may help address access barriers and improve vaccination coverage among Medicaid recipients, particularly for HPV and other routine vaccines.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and reliance on claims data, which may not capture all vaccinations or account for potential confounding factors. The evidence is moderate, as it provides trend data but does not establish causality or address all barriers to vaccination.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective claims analysis examined trends in pharmacy-based vaccination among Medicaid recipients aged 9 years or older in the United States from 2018 to 2023. The study found that overall vaccination rates for HPV, influenza, and other routine vaccines declined during this period, though the proportion of vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased, particularly among adults aged 19-49. Pharmacy-based vaccination rose by 5.2-17.5 percentage points for several vaccines, including HPV. The authors suggest that pharmacies may help mitigate access barriers, though disparities persisted across racial and ethnic groups. The evidence is moderate due to the retrospective design and reliance on claims data, limiting causal inference.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 医疗补助受益人经常面临 疫苗接种 的障碍,包括访问受限,这导致 疫苗接种 比率较低。该研究旨在评估基于药房的 疫苗接种 设置是否可以减轻这些障碍并改善该人群中的 疫苗接种 趋势。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这是对 2018 年 1 月 1 日至 2023 年 12 月 31 日期间 9 岁或以上医疗补助接受者中基于药房的 疫苗接种 趋势的回顾性分析。该研究评估了药房服用 疫苗接种 的百分比以及随时间推移的总体 疫苗接种 比率。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究确定了在药房服用的所有 疫苗接种 的百分比,并计算了 疫苗接种 比率的总体百分比变化。它按年龄和种族或民族分析了趋势,重点关注常规和季节性 疫苗。
elements_zh.main_results: 大多数 疫苗 的总体常规和季节性 疫苗接种 发病率在 2023 年仍然低于 2018-2019 年,包括青少年的 HPV、流感和 Tdap/Td,以及成人的甲型肝炎、流感、脑膜炎球菌、肺炎球菌和 Tdap/Td。在药房服用 疫苗接种 的成年人比例有所增加,19-49 岁人群中含有甲型肝炎、乙型肝炎、HPV、脑膜炎球菌、肺炎球菌和破伤风的 疫苗 的比例增加了 5.2-17.5 个百分点。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出的结论是,虽然医疗补助受益人的 疫苗接种 总体比率下降,但在药房服用 疫苗接种 的比例有所增加,这表明通过药房设置的获取情况有所改善。这一趋势在白人参与者中最为明显,在 65 岁及以上的成年人中差异较小。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,扩大基于药房的 疫苗接种 服务可能有助于解决获取障碍并提高医疗补助接受者的 疫苗接种 覆盖率,特别是针对 HPV 和其他常规 疫苗。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计和对索赔数据的依赖而受到限制,这些数据可能无法捕获所有 疫苗接种 或解释潜在的混杂因素。证据是中等的,因为它提供了趋势数据,但没有建立因果关系或解决 疫苗接种 的所有障碍。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Medicaid beneficiaries often face barriers to vaccination, including limited access, which contributes to low vaccination rates. The study aimed to assess whether pharmacy-based vaccination settings could mitigate these barriers and improve vaccination trends among this population.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This was a retrospective analysis of trends in pharmacy-based vaccination among Medicaid recipients aged 9 years or older from 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2023. The study evaluated the percentage of vaccinations administered at pharmacies and overall vaccination rates over time.
analysis_en.methods: The study determined the percentage of all vaccinations administered at pharmacies and calculated the overall percentage change in vaccination rates. It analyzed trends by age and race or ethnicity, focusing on routine and seasonal vaccines.
analysis_en.main_results: Overall routine and seasonal vaccination rates remained lower in 2023 than in 2018-2019 for most vaccines, including HPV, influenza, and Tdap/Td in adolescents, and hepatitis A, influenza, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and Tdap/Td in adults. The percentage of vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased among adults, with gains of 5.2-17.5 percentage points for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, HPV, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and tetanus-containing vaccines in those aged 19-49.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that while overall vaccination rates declined among Medicaid beneficiaries, the proportion of vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased, suggesting improved access through pharmacy settings. This trend was most pronounced in White enrollees, with smaller differentials in adults aged 65 and older.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that expanding pharmacy-based vaccination services may help address access barriers and improve vaccination coverage among Medicaid recipients, particularly for HPV and other routine vaccines.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and reliance on claims data, which may not capture all vaccinations or account for potential confounding factors. The evidence is moderate, as it provides trend data but does not establish causality or address all barriers to vaccination.

papers.title_zh: 2018-2023 年美国医疗补助受益人药房和医疗环境中 疫苗接种 的趋势:索赔分析。
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Medicaid beneficiaries typically have low vaccination rates, in part due to limited access. Pharmacies provide easy-to-access locations for vaccination. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: This was a retrospective analysis of trends in pharmacy-based vaccination by age and race or ethnicity among Medicaid recipients aged ≥9 from 1 January 2018 (before the COVID-19 pandemic) to 31 December 2023. The percentage of all vaccinations administered at pharmacies and the overall percentage change in vaccination rates were determined. RESULTS: With some exceptions, overall routine and seasonal vaccination rates remained lower in 2023 than in 2018-2019. This was observed for human papillomavirus (HPV), influenza, and tetanus-containing (Tdap/Td) vaccines in adolescents and for hepatitis A, influenza, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and Tdap/Td vaccines in various adult age groups. The percentage of routine and seasonal vaccinations administered at pharmacies increased over the study period among adults, with increases of 5.2-17.5 percentage points for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, HPV, meningococcal, pneumococcal, and tetanus-containing vaccines among those aged 19-49. Across age groups, pharmacy-based vaccination was most frequent in White enrollees, followed by Black and then Hispanic enrollees, with smaller differentials in adults aged ≥65. CONCLUSIONS: Generally overall vaccine administration rates declined in Medicaid beneficiaries; however, the proportion administered at pharmacies increased.

news.content_zh: 国际癌症研究机构 (IARC) 及其合作机构已获得一笔赠款,用于加强冲突地区的 宫颈癌 预防工作。该倡议是 IARC 更广泛使命的一部分,旨在促进全球癌症预防并解决医疗保健获取方面的差异。这笔赠款旨在改善医疗基础设施经常受到损害、导致对该疾病的认识和信息有限的地区的 宫颈癌 预防。虽然证据中没有详细说明赠款影响的确切范围和规模,但重点是处于危险之中的人群,特别是育龄妇女。该活动已被确认为官方资助奖项,并且没有提及任何不确定性或未解决的信息。该倡议反映了国际癌症研究机构致力于通过有针对性的研究和能力建设努力应对弱势社区与癌症相关的挑战。

Western Pacific Papua New Guinea Global Regions WHO Regional websites Africa Americas South-East Asia Europe Eastern Mediterranean Western Pacific Countries Countries, territories and areas in the WHO Western Pacific Region: American Samoa (USA) * Australia Brunei Darussalam Cambodia China Cook Islands Fiji French Polynesia (France) Guam (USA) * Hong Kong SAR (China) Indonesia Japan Kiribati Lao People's Democratic Republic Macao SAR (China) Malaysia Marshall Islands Micronesia, Federated States of Mongolia Naoero New Caledonia (France) New Zealand Niue Northern Mariana Islands (USA) * Palau Papua New Guinea Philippines Pitcairn Islands (UK) Republic of Korea Samoa Singapore Solomon Islands Tokelau Tonga Tuvalu Vanuatu Viet Nam Wallis and Futuna (France) Home Health topics Our work News Emergencies About us Home Health topics Our work News Emergencies About us Home/ News/ Detail/ Papua New Guinea takes a major step to protect girls and women from cervical cancer © WHO / Glenda Gonzales The first shipment of HPV vaccines for Papua New Guinea, marking the start of a nationwide effort to protect girls from cervical cancer. © Credits Papua New Guinea takes a major step to protect girls and women from cervical cancer 11 August 2026 News release Papua New Guinea Reading time: 2 min (535 words) Papua New Guinea has reached an important milestone in the fight against cervical cancer with the arrival of its first shipment of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines. The country recently received 100 000 vaccine vials, marking the beginning of a nationwide effort to protect girls from one of the leading causes of cancer deaths among women in Papua New Guinea. A further 180 000 vaccine vials are expected to arrive in the coming months, bringing the total supply to 280 000 vials. The introduction of the HPV vaccine into Papua New Guinea's national immunization programme represents a significant investment in the health and well-being of future generations of women. Cervical cancer remains a major public health challenge in the country, with hundreds of women losing their lives to a disease that is largely preventable. Vaccination offers one of the most effective ways to reduce this burden and save lives. The HPV is a common virus that can cause cervical cancer. While many HPV infections resolve naturally, some types of the virus can lead to changes in cervical cells that may develop into cancer over time. The HPV vaccine protects girls before they are exposed to the virus, helping prevent cervical cancer later in life. The vaccine has a strong global safety record and plays a critical role in the global effort to eliminate cervical cancer. HPV vaccines. © WHO / Glenda Gonzales The first phase of the programme is expected to begin on 10 September 2026 and will target approximately 60 000 girls aged 9 to 14 years during the first phase of the national rollout. As additional vaccine supplies arrive and implementation capacity increases, the programme will progressively expand to more provinces, helping ensure girls across the country can access this life-saving protection. This achievement reflects strong leadership from the Government of Papua New Guinea, which has allocated PGK 6.2 million in the 2026 National Budget to support the introduction of the HPV vaccine. The National Department of Health, working closely with the National Department of Education and Provincial Health Authorities, is leading the planning and delivery of the programme. The rollout is also the result of a strong partnership between the Government of Papua New Guinea and global health partners. The World Health Organization (WHO) is providing technical support for policy development, programme planning, health worker training, and monitoring and evaluation. UNICEF is supporting vaccine procurement and delivery, cold chain and supply systems, programme planning and engagement with families and communities. Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, is providing vital co-financing support to help make the programme possible. © WHO Papua New Guinea Together, these partners are working to ensure that girls across Papua New Guinea have access to safe, effective protection against cervical cancer. Their collaboration demonstrates what can be achieved when governments and development partners work together towards a shared public health goal. The introduction of HPV vaccination is an important step towards a future where fewer women develop cervical cancer and fewer families experience the loss of mothers, daughters, sisters and loved ones to a preventable disease. By investing in prevention today, Papua New Guinea is helping protect the health of future generations and moving closer to a world free from cervical cancer

news.content: MD University Rohtak study flags HPV-16,18 in cervical cancer patients, stresses early screening Researchers also identified factors like age at first childbirth, number of births, miscarriages and lifestyle-related factors as being associated with cervical cancer risk A research study by the Department of Genetics at Maharshi Dayanand University (MDU), Rohtak, has underlined the crucial role of HPV screening and early detection in the fight against cervical cancer, with high-risk HPV types 16 and 18 found in a majority of the patients studied. The study was conducted by research scholar Shalu under the supervision of Prof Ritu Yadav, Department of Genetics, MDU, with Prof Meenakshi Chauhan of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, PGIMS, Rohtak, as co-supervisor. The researchers also identified factors such as age at first childbirth, number of births, miscarriages and lifestyle-related factors as being associated with cervical cancer risk, said Pankaj Nain, Public Relations Officer, MDU. He maintained that the study further examined molecular changes in long non-coding RNAs and identified certain genetic and epigenetic alterations that could potentially serve as biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis. The findings could help pave the way for personalised treatment and newer therapeutic approaches. “Prof Ritu Yadav has been actively promoting awareness about cervical cancer across North India. Through awareness programmes, more than 2,000 women from rural and urban areas have so far been sensitised to the symptoms, risk factors, prevention and importance of timely screening. She stressed that HPV vaccination, regular screening and awareness are key to reducing the burden of cervical cancer,” the PRO added

news.source_body_en: A study conducted by the Department of Genetics at MD University, Rohtak, has highlighted the significant role of high-risk HPV types 16 and 18 in cervical cancer. The research, led by Shalu under the supervision of Prof Ritu Yadav and co-supervised by Prof Meenakshi Chauhan, found that these HPV types were present in a majority of cervical cancer patients. The study also examined molecular changes in long non-coding RNAs and identified genetic and epigenetic alterations that could serve as biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis. These findings could potentially lead to personalized treatment and new therapeutic approaches. Additionally, the researchers emphasized the importance of early screening and awareness programs, which have already sensitized over 2,000 women in rural and urban areas to the symptoms, risk factors, and prevention of cervical cancer. Prof Ritu Yadav has been actively promoting awareness about cervical cancer across North India, underscoring the need for HPV vaccination, regular screening, and public education.
news.content_zh: Rohtak 马里兰大学遗传学系进行的一项研究强调了 高危型HPV 16 型和 18 型在 宫颈癌 中的重要作用。这项由 Shalu 领导、Ritu Yadav 教授和 Meenakshi Chauhan 教授共同监督的研究发现,大多数 宫颈癌 患者体内都存在这些 HPV 类型。该研究还检查了长非编码 RNA 的分子变化,并确定了可以作为早期 诊断 和预后的生物标志物的遗传和表观遗传改变。这些发现可能会带来个性化的 治疗 和新的治疗方法。此外,研究人员强调了早期筛查和宣传计划的重要性,这些计划已经使农村和城市地区的 2,000 多名女性对 宫颈癌 的症状、危险因素和预防有了认识。Ritu Yadav 教授一直在印度北部积极提高人们对 宫颈癌 的认识,强调 HPV 疫苗接种、定期筛查和公共教育的必要性。

news.content: HPV self-testing expands cervical cancer screening Earlier detection could reduce deaths from the disease in high-risk, underscreened populations. Media Contact: Vishva Nalamalapu - vnala@uw.edu Offering human papilloma virus (HPV) self-testing at an opioid treatment program increased cervical cancer screening among patients who often go without it, according to research published in July's JAMA Network Open. Expanded screening could help people detect cervical cancer at earlier stages and could reduce mortality as a result. “We have to get out into new environments to reach patients who are not being reached through standard testing,” said Elizabeth Swisher, a professor of gynecologic oncology at the University of Washington School of Medicine and the study’s lead author. Swisher cares for patients with advanced stage cervical cancer, which often stems from HPV infections. She has grown frustrated, she said, that a lack of access to early HPV screening results in many patients needing intense medical therapies and facing high mortality risk. People who are marginalized from the healthcare system, such as those with opioid use disorder, are more likely to be unscreened. People with opioid use disorder also have higher risk factors for cervical cancer. “This is a very underscreened patient population and a high-risk patient population,” said Swisher. Swisher’s team partnered with We Care Daily Clinics, an opioid-treatment program that also provides holistic care, to offer HPV self-testing to their patients. During patients’ annual wellness visits, Swisher's team offered testing to everyone 25 or older who had a cervix and was overdue for screening or unsure when they were last screened. Screening has traditionally been done through a pelvic exam, but the team gave patients a vaginal swab to self-screen. This approach is just as accurate as a clinician-administered screen, can be done in locations without gynecological services, and is more comfortable for many patients. When test results were positive for high-risk HPV strains, the clinic connected those patients with follow-up care ranging from a Pap smear, which collects cells from the cervix, to a colposcopy, which uses a magnifying instrument to look at the cervix. Most people with earlier stages of cervical cancer can get the cancerous tissue removed. For people whose disease is at a later stage, treatment usually involves radiation and chemotherapy. Swisher’s team found that 90% of patients were due for screening. Of those, 90% wanted to self-screen. The patients' swabs showed nearly double the rate of positive, high-risk HPV, compared to a recent large cervical cancer screening study in Washington. HPV self-testing was an easy process for both clinic staff and patients. Connecting patients with follow-up care was a challenge, but overall, offering self-testing in the clinic was an important first step to expand screening, Swisher said. “Screening the unscreened will make an impact on cervical cancer mortality,” she said. Her team is hoping this service will expand to more opioid-treatment programs and other clinics serving underscreened populations, such as farmworkers and unhoused people. “This could become a standard offering.” The research was funded by Cancer Center Support Grant P30 CA015704 from the NCI of the NIH. Related: HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer before it starts For details about UW Medicine, please see our About page

Swisher’s team partnered with We Care Daily Clinics, an opioid-treatment program that also provides holistic care, to offer HPV self-testing to their patients. During patients’ annual wellness visits, Swisher's team offered testing to everyone 25 or older who had a cervix and was overdue for screening or unsure when they were last screened. Screening has traditionally been done through a pelvic exam, but the team gave patients a vaginal swab to self-screen. This approach is just as accurate as a clinician-administered screen, can be done in locations without gynecological services, and is more comfortable for many patients. When test results were positive for high-risk HPV strains, the clinic connected those patients with follow-up care ranging from a Pap smear, which collects cells from the cervix, to a colposcopy, which uses a magnifying instrument to look at the cervix. Most people with earlier stages of cervical cancer can get the cancerous tissue removed. For people whose disease is at a later stage, treatment usually involves radiation and chemotherapy. Swisher’s team found that 90% of patients were due for screening. Of those, 90% wanted to self-screen. The patients' swabs showed nearly double the rate of positive, high-risk HPV, compared to a recent large cervical cancer screening study in Washington. HPV self-testing was an easy process for both clinic staff and patients. Connecting patients with follow-up care was a challenge, but overall, offering self-testing in the clinic was an important first step to expand screening, Swisher said. “Screening the unscreened will make an impact on cervical cancer mortality,” she said. Her team is hoping this service will expand to more opioid-treatment programs and other clinics serving underscreened populations, such as farmworkers and unhoused people. “This could become a standard offering.” The research was funded by Cancer Center Support Grant P30 CA015704 from the NCI of the NIH. news.content: SECTIONS journalism with a human touch Login My Profile Signed In as Profile Change Password Sign out Home Magazine Quick Read India World Sports Business Entertainment Reviews Columns Leisure More Hamburger Web Stories Videos Sci/Tech Health Defence Middle East Maritime Tourism Education Jobs & Career Search Subscribe Specials Middle East Defence Health Maritime × Search results for journalism with a human touch × News India World Sports Business Tourism Sci/Tech Entertainment Jobs & Career Magazine The Week Health Opinion Specials Health Defence Middle East Maritime Reviews Movies Books Gadgets Games Multimedia Videos Web Stories Quick Read Leisure Society Lifestyle Services About Us Privacy Policy Terms of Use Contact Us SIGN IN SUBSCRIBE Follow Us News Health Beyond cervical cancer: 5 diseases the HPV vaccine can actually prevent HPV vaccine benefits extend well beyond cervical cancer, offering crucial protection against a range of other cancers and conditions in all genders Dr Aruna Kalra Published: August 09, 2026 11:27 AM IST 3 minute Read Share × Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Reddit 0 Comments Link Copied Highlights Vaccination is most effective when administered to adolescents before any exposure to the virus Unlike cervical cancer, there is no routine screening for throat cancer, making vaccination the most effective form of prevention for boys and men HPV is a leading cause of throat cancers, which now affect more men than women have cervical cancer in some countries Ask most people what the HPV vaccine is for, and the answer will almost always be the same: cervical cancer. It is not a wrong answer — but it is an incomplete one, and doctors say this narrow understanding is quietly costing lives. Human papillomavirus is not a women's health issue confined to one organ. It is a common virus that moves silently between people, and its consequences reach far wider than most patients, and even some clinicians in general conversation, tend to acknowledge. The vaccine was introduced under the banner of cervical cancer prevention, and understandably so — it remains the most visible and most studied benefit, a practising physician explains. But that framing has, in some ways, boxed the vaccine into a single narrative. Parents of sons often assume it isn't relevant to them. That assumption is simply incorrect. Here is what the conversation usually leaves out. 1. Oropharyngeal (throat) cancers HPV is now recognised as a leading cause of cancers at the back of the throat, tonsils and base of the tongue — and in several countries, these cases in men have overtaken cervical cancer cases in women. Unlike cervical cancer, there is no routine screening test for throat cancer, which makes prevention through vaccination considerably more valuable, not less. 2. Anal cancer Anal cancer linked to HPV affects both men and women, though certain groups carry a disproportionately higher risk. It is rarely discussed openly, largely due to stigma rather than rarity, and doctors argue that this silence is precisely why awareness campaigns tend to skip over it. 3. Penile cancer A less common but genuinely preventable disease, penile cancer is strongly associated with HPV infection. Its omission from most public vaccine messaging reinforces the myth that HPV vaccination is a "female" intervention, when the virus itself makes no such distinction. 4. Vulvar and vaginal cancers These cancers receive comparatively little attention, overshadowed entirely by their more widely publicised cervical counterpart. Yet a substantial proportion of cases are directly attributable to HPV, and are equally preventable through timely vaccination. 5. Genital warts Not life-threatening, but far from trivial. Genital warts caused by HPV can be persistent, distressing and costly to treat, and they affect a meaningful share of sexually active adults. Doctors note that this is often the first, and sometimes only, tangible benefit patients notice after vaccination programmes take hold in a population. The consultant is careful to add a note of nuance here: not every strain of HPV causes cancer, and not every case of cancer at these sites is HPV-related. "The vaccine isn't a blanket shield against all disease at these locations — it targets specific high-risk strains. But those strains do the overwhelming share of the damage, which is exactly why prevention matters so much." What ties all five conditions together, doctors stress, is timing. The vaccine works best when given before exposure to the virus — typically recommended for adolescents of any gender, well before the onset of sexual activity — though catch-up vaccination remains worthwhile for many young adults. Perhaps the most persistent myth of all is that HPV vaccination is a women's health decision. It isn't. It is a shared, preventable-disease conversation that concerns sons as much as daughters, and one that deserves to be had earlier, more openly, and with considerably more accuracy than it currently is. The author is the Director - Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Director Academics - Robotic Gynaecology, CK Birla Hospital, Gurgaon. news.content: 首页 HOME 产经 INDUSTRY 地产 ESTATE 股票 STOCK 新股 IPO 基金 FUND 理财 MONEY 外汇 FOREX 期货 FUTURES 数据 DATA 内线 VIP 搜索 SEARCH 万泰生物(603392):万泰生物关于公司九价HPV疫苗获得泰国上市许可 时间:2026年08月11日 16:56:34 中财网 原标题:万泰生物:万泰生物关于公司九价HPV疫苗获得泰国上市许可的公告 证券代码:603392 证券简称:万泰生物 公告编号:2026-039 北京万泰生物药业股份有限公司 关于公司九价 HPV疫苗获得泰国上市许可的公告 本公司董事会及全体董事保证本公告内容不存在任何虚假记载、误导性陈述或者重大遗漏,并对其内容的真实性、准确性和完整性承担法律责任。 近日,北京万泰生物药业股份有限公司(以下简称“公司”)全资子公司厦门万泰沧海生物技术有限公司(以下简称“万泰沧海”)自主研发的九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗(大肠埃希菌)(以下简称“九价HPV疫苗”)获得泰国食品药品监督管理局批准。现将相关信息公告如下: 一、药品基本信息 药品名称:九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗(大肠埃希菌)(英文名称:RecombinantHuman Papillomavirus 9-Valent(Types 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52,58)Vaccine(Escherichiacoli) 剂型:注射剂 规格:0.5mL/剂 二、药品其他信息 九价HPV疫苗为万泰沧海自主研发的预防用生物制品,已于2025年获得国家药品监督管理局颁发的药品注册证书,为我国首款、全球第二款九价HPV疫苗,主要适用于9-45岁女性,覆盖HPV16/18/31/33/45/52/58七种高危型和HPV6/11两种低危型,可预防上述型别人乳头瘤病毒感染引起的相关疾病。 三、对公司的影响及风险提示 本次九价HPV疫苗在泰国获批,是该产品取得的首个境外上市许可,标志着该产品已具备出口至泰国市场的资质。本次获批不仅为公司在泰国市场的业务拓展奠定了坚实基础,更将对公司持续拓展东南亚市场产生积极而深远的影响。 结合公司二价HPV疫苗已取得的国际化成果,公司正构建从二价到九价、从公共卫生采购到商业化销售的全球化疫苗网络,进一步提升公司在国际市场的品牌影响力和竞争力。 然而,九价HPV疫苗未来在境外的销售情况可能受到政策环境变化、市场推广、客户需求、市场竞争等多重因素影响,存在不确定性。 公司将持续推进九价HPV疫苗在海外国家的注册申报,相关申报能否获得批准及获得批准的时间尚存在不确定性。公司未来将按照相关规定在定期报告中披露在相关市场获得上市许可的情况。 敬请广大投资者谨慎决策,注意防范投资风险。 特此公告。 北京万泰生物药业股份有限公司董事会 原标题:万泰生物:万泰生物关于公司九价HPV疫苗获得泰国上市许可的公告 证券代码:603392 证券简称:万泰生物 公告编号:2026-039 北京万泰生物药业股份有限公司 关于公司九价 HPV疫苗获得泰国上市许可的公告 本公司董事会及全体董事保证本公告内容不存在任何虚假记载、误导性陈述或者重大遗漏,并对其内容的真实性、准确性和完整性承担法律责任。 近日,北京万泰生物药业股份有限公司(以下简称“公司”)全资子公司厦门万泰沧海生物技术有限公司(以下简称“万泰沧海”)自主研发的九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗(大肠埃希菌)(以下简称“九价HPV疫苗”)获得泰国食品药品监督管理局批准。现将相关信息公告如下: 一、药品基本信息 药品名称:九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗(大肠埃希菌)(英文名称:RecombinantHuman Papillomavirus 9-Valent(Types 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52,58)Vaccine(Escherichiacoli) 剂型:注射剂 规格:0.5mL/剂 二、药品其他信息 九价HPV疫苗为万泰沧海自主研发的预防用生物制品,已于2025年获得国家药品监督管理局颁发的药品注册证书,为我国首款、全球第二款九价HPV疫苗,主要适用于9-45岁女性,覆盖HPV16/18/31/33/45/52/58七种高危型和HPV6/11两种低危型,可预防上述型别人乳头瘤病毒感染引起的相关疾病。 三、对公司的影响及风险提示 本次九价HPV疫苗在泰国获批,是该产品取得的首个境外上市许可,标志着该产品已具备出口至泰国市场的资质。本次获批不仅为公司在泰国市场的业务拓展奠定了坚实基础,更将对公司持续拓展东南亚市场产生积极而深远的影响。 结合公司二价HPV疫苗已取得的国际化成果,公司正构建从二价到九价、从公共卫生采购到商业化销售的全球化疫苗网络,进一步提升公司在国际市场的品牌影响力和竞争力。 然而,九价HPV疫苗未来在境外的销售情况可能受到政策环境变化、市场推广、客户需求、市场竞争等多重因素影响,存在不确定性。 公司将持续推进九价HPV疫苗在海外国家的注册申报,相关申报能否获得批准及获得批准的时间尚存在不确定性。公司未来将按照相关规定在定期报告中披露在相关市场获得上市许可的情况。 敬请广大投资者谨慎决策,注意防范投资风险。 特此公告。 北京万泰生物药业股份有限公司董事会 analysis.brief_en: On 11 August 2026, Beijing Wantai Biological Pharmacy Enterprise announced that its nine-valent HPV vaccine, produced by its Xiamen subsidiary, has received marketing authorization from Thailand’s regulator. The Escherichia coli–based vaccine targets nine oncogenic and low-risk HPV types and is indicated for females aged 9–45. This marks the first overseas approval for the product and supports the company’s push to expand into Southeast Asia. Wantai stated the approval strengthens its global vaccine network and brand presence, while noting that future sales and additional country registrations remain uncertain due to policy, market, and competitive factors.

Health Scientists create chewing gum that could protect high-risk people from mouth and throat cancer By Rachel Sacks Published Aug. 10, 2026, 1:43 p.m. ET Comments 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE See more of our coverage in your search results. Add The New York Post on Google Chew on this news. Scientists may have developed an easy way to stop one of the most aggressive and common forms of head and neck cancer that often starts in the mouth and throat. And all it would take is popping a piece of bioengineered bean gum. Reducing one of the most aggressive and common head and neck cancers may be as easy as popping a piece of gum. Africa Studio – stock.adobe.com Accounting for 90% of all head and neck cancers, squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common type of skin cancer in the US. However, many current treatments have shown limited effectiveness, prompting researchers at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania to create a better therapy. The result, published in Scientific Reports, was a bioengineered gum made from lablab beans — a species of bean also known as hyacinth beans — that sharply reduced one virus and two types of bacteria linked to the disease. Building on previous work creating a chewing gum made from bean gum and containing a naturally antiviral protein FRIL, researchers tested oral samples of patients for three microbes associated with cancer. These included human papillomavirus (HPV) and two bacterial species, Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn). The increase in mouth and throat cancer has been strongly linked to HPV infection, accounting for 60% to 75% of cases. High-risk HPV types like HPV 16, HPV 18 and HPV 59 are the most likely to result in squamous carcinoma. A bioengineered bean gum greatly reduced levels of one virus and two types of bacteria linked to squamous cell cancer. Kevin Monko/Penn Dental Medicine “And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies,” lead researcher Henry Daniell said in a press release. The bean gum extracts reduced HPV by 93% in saliva samples and 80% in oral rinse samples. When protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide that kills harmful bacteria, was added to the gum, a single dose reduced Pg and Fn levels to nearly zero. Notably, the addition of protegrin also didn’t affect beneficial bacteria found in the mouth, contrasting with radiation therapy, which reduces good bacteria and increases disease-causing yeast. Researchers believe the gum’s ability to target dangerous microbes while preserving healthy oral microbiome could be useful as an additional therapy along with current treatments or as a preventive measure. “Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission,” Daniell said. Previous studies have found that daily oral maintenance — regularly brushing and flossing — could drastically reduce the chances of developing head and neck cancers. What do you think? Post a comment. These healthy habits could potentially reduce more than a dozen species of bacteria that increase the risk of squamous cell carcinoma. This came on the heels of the American Cancer Society declaring that 40% of cancer cases and nearly half of cancer deaths in American adults 30 and older could be prevented with a lifestyle change. news.content: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) shows substantial intra- and inter-tumoral heterogeneity. We mapped tumor architecture across HPV-positive and HPV-negative HNSCC through spatial transcriptomics ( n = 26). HPV-positive tumors display hypercellularity, higher lymphocyte presence, enriched hypoxia and reduced partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (p-EMT) in malignant cells. We observed two distinct spatial architectures of p-EMT: p-EMT edge, where p-EMT is coupled to fibroblasts at the invasive front via TGFβ, and p-EMT core, in which tumor-infiltrating immunosuppressive macrophages and neutrophils induce p-EMT via oncostatin M in the core of tumor nests. These two p-EMT patterns were consistent across multiple samples from the same tumor, suggesting they are tumor-wide features. Together, these findings reveal that distinct interactions in the tumor microenvironment converge on a similar p-EMT cellular phenotype, but in a different spatial pattern that may have potential biological and clinical implications for our understanding of invasion, immune modulation and new targeted therapeutics for HNSCC. Previously published datasets used for survival analyses are publicly available from the following sources: TCGA-HNSC bulk RNA-seq and clinical data are available through the Broad Institute Genome Data Analysis Center Firehose; microarray expression and clinical data from the Leipzig HNSCC cohort are available from the National Center for Biotechnology Information Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE65858 ; and microarray expression and clinical data from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center cohort are available from the National Center for Biotechnology Information Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE41613 . analysis.brief_en: A Nature study published on 14 August 2026 used spatial transcriptomics on 26 head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) samples to map tumor architecture in HPV-positive and HPV-negative tumors. Researchers identified two distinct spatial patterns of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (p-EMT): an 'edge' pattern linked to fibroblast interactions via TGFβ at invasive fronts, and a 'core' pattern driven by immunosuppressive macrophages and neutrophils via oncostatin M within tumor nests. These patterns were consistent across multiple samples from the same tumor, suggesting tumor-wide features with potential biological and clinical implications for invasion, immune evasion, and targeted therapies. All datasets and analysis code are publicly accessible, but the findings remain preliminary and require further validation.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 14 日发表的《自然》研究使用 26 个头颈鳞状细胞癌 (HNSCC) 样本的空间转录组学来绘制 HPV 阳性和 HPV 阴性肿瘤的肿瘤结构图。研究人员发现了部分上皮间质转化(p-EMT)的两种不同的空间模式:一种“边缘”模式,与侵入前沿通过 TGFβ 与成纤维细胞相互作用相关;另一种“核心”模式,由免疫抑制性巨噬细胞和中性粒细胞通过肿瘤巢内的制瘤素 M 驱动。这些模式在同一肿瘤的多个样本中是一致的,表明肿瘤范围的特征对侵袭、免疫逃避和靶向治疗具有潜在的生物学和临床意义。所有数据集和分析代码均可公开访问,但研究结果仍处于初步阶段,需要进一步验证。

Far fewer know that the same virus is now one of the leading causes of throat cancer, and that infections in both parts of the body are transmitted, and switch on cancer, in strikingly similar ways. As Ghana rolls out its first nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for adolescent girls, it is worth understanding why this one virus deserves attention well beyond the cervix. A virus with more than 200 faces HPV is not a single virus but a family of more than 200 related viruses that infect skin and mucous membranes. Most types are harmless and clear on their own within one to two years. A smaller group, classified as "high-risk" types, can persist in the body and gradually push infected cells toward cancer. Two of these, HPV-16 and HPV-18, are responsible for the majority of HPV-related cancers worldwide, including most cervical cancers and a large share of oropharyngeal (throat) cancers. HPV spreads through direct skin-to-skin and mucosal contact during vaginal, anal, and oral sex. It does not require the exchange of bodily fluids the way HIV or hepatitis B does, which is part of why it is the most common sexually transmitted infection globally, and why condoms, though protective, do not eliminate risk entirely since they don't cover all exposed skin. Oral sex: the specific route into the throat Because oropharyngeal cancer is the less familiar of the two diseases, it is worth being precise about how HPV actually gets into the throat, since the evidence here comes from some of the largest behavioural studies conducted on the subject. The clearest data come from a landmark U.S. case-control study led by epidemiologist Gypsyamber D'Souza and colleagues, which compared 100 patients with oropharyngeal cancer to 200 matched cancer-free controls. Among the patients with cancer, 88 percent reported having had at least one lifetime oral-sex partner, and oral HPV-16 infection was found in 32 percent of cancer patients versus just 4 percent of controls, while any oral HPV infection was found in 37 percent of patients versus 6 percent of controls. That study was central to establishing oral sex, specifically, rather than sexual activity in general, as a driver of this cancer. Discover more Medical Literature & Resources cancers cancer A larger follow-up study by the same research group, published in 2021 and covering 163 oropharyngeal cancer patients and 345 matched controls, found that people with more than 10 lifetime oral-sex partners had over four times the odds of developing HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer compared with those with fewer partners. The same study found that starting oral sex before age 18, having oral sex with partners at least ten years older, and having a higher "intensity" of oral-sex partners over a short period were each independently linked to higher risk, on top of partner count alone. National survey data collected in the United States (NHANES) similarly show a clear gradient: oral HPV was found in fewer than 2.5 percent of people who reported never having performed oral sex, rising to as much as 14 to 15 percent among men who had both smoked and had five or more lifetime oral-sex partners. Across that same national dataset, men were roughly six times more likely than women to carry oncogenic oral HPV, which lines up with the fact that HPV-related throat cancer affects men several times more often than women worldwide. None of this means oral sex is unusually dangerous compared to other forms of sexual contact, or that people who have had oral sex will develop cancer; the great majority of oral HPV infections, like cervical ones, clear on their own. What the data show is a dose-response relationship: the more lifetime oral-sex exposure to HPV a person has, particularly starting at a younger age or with more partners, the higher their cumulative risk of a persistent infection that could, over decades, progress to cancer. The same molecular hijack, two different addresses What links cervical cancer and HPV-driven throat cancer is not just the virus's name, but its precise mechanism of harm. When a high-risk HPV type infects the basal cells of the cervix or the tissue lining the tonsils and base of the tongue, it produces two small viral proteins, E6 and E7, that hijack the host cell's own safety systems. Ordinarily, a cell has built-in checkpoints that stop damaged or abnormally dividing cells from surviving and multiplying. The E6 protein binds to and marks for destruction a tumour-suppressor protein called p53, often described as the "guardian of the genome," which would otherwise force damaged cells to stop dividing or self-destruct. Around the same time, the E7 protein disables another checkpoint protein, the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which normally keeps cells from dividing until they are ready. With both brakes released, infected cells are pushed to keep dividing even as genetic damage accumulates, and cells that should have died instead survive, replicate, and can eventually pass this instability on to daughter cells. Over years, this can progress from precancerous changes to invasive cancer. Discover more infection infections HEALTH Because this E6/E7 mechanism is the same whether the infected tissue is cervical epithelium or the lymphoid tissue of the tonsils and tongue base, HPV-driven cervical cancer and HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer are, at the molecular level, closely related diseases arising in different organs. Where the two cancers diverge Despite the shared mechanism, the two cancers differ in important ways that matter for prevention and detection. Cervical cancer overwhelmingly affects women and has a well-established screening pathway: Pap smears and HPV DNA tests can catch precancerous cervical changes years before they become cancer, which is why organised screening programmes have driven down cervical cancer rates wherever they have been sustained. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer, by contrast, disproportionately affects men, and there is no equivalent routine screening test for the throat. Research tracking cancer registries has found that HPV-positive throat cancers have risen sharply in higher-income countries over the past two decades, even as tobacco-related throat cancers have declined, so that HPV is now estimated to cause a majority of oropharyngeal cancers in some developed countries. Because there is no early-warning test, these cancers are often diagnosed only after a person notices a persistent sore throat, difficulty swallowing, an unexplained lump in the neck, or ear pain that does not resolve, symptoms easy to dismiss until the disease is more advanced. As the data above show, risk rises specifically with the number and pattern of oral-sex partners, and is compounded further by smoking and a weakened immune system, all of which make it harder for the body to clear a persistent high-risk HPV infection before it can trigger these changes. The burden, in numbers Cervical cancer remains the fourth most common cancer in women globally, with roughly 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths a year, around 90 percent of them in low- and middle-income countries. In Ghana specifically, there were an estimated 3,072 new cervical cancer cases in 2023. Across sub-Saharan Africa, the burden is especially heavy: the region records well over 117,000 new cervical cancer cases and more than 76,000 deaths annually, the highest incidence of any region in the world, largely because screening and vaccination coverage have historically lagged behind higher-income countries. Throat cancer's HPV story is a more recent one. Global estimates attribute roughly 30 to 43 percent of oropharyngeal cancers to HPV infection, with some high-income countries reporting figures well above that. In the United States, HPV-positive throat cancer cases rose by more than 200 percent between 1988 and 2004, and HPV is now believed to cause around 70 percent of oropharyngeal cancers in similar developed-country settings. Men are consistently affected several times more often than women. Why this matters for Ghana right now In October 2025, Ghana Health Service, together with Gavi, the WHO, and UNICEF, launched the country's first nationwide HPV vaccination campaign, aiming to reach about 2.4 million girls aged 9 to 14 with a vaccine that is now being folded into the routine immunisation schedule. This is expected to prevent tens of thousands of future cervical cancer deaths, and it lines up Ghana with the WHO's global target of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem by pushing incidence below 4 cases per 100,000 women. What is less discussed locally is that the same vaccine also protects against the HPV types responsible for most throat cancers, and current guidance supports vaccinating boys as well as girls, since men bear a disproportionate share of the HPV-related throat cancer burden and unvaccinated men also continue to transmit the virus. A vaccination conversation framed only around "protecting girls from cervical cancer" leaves out half the picture, and half the population that could benefit. What actually works The core prevention message is genuinely simple, even if the biology behind it is complex: Get the HPV vaccine, ideally before the start of sexual activity, since it works best before a person is exposed to the virus. In Ghana, this is now free for eligible girls through the national programme. Attend cervical screening on the recommended schedule if you are a woman old enough to be eligible; it remains the only proven way to catch cervical changes before they become cancer. Practise safer sex, including barrier protection during oral sex and being mindful that risk rises with the number of oral-sex partners and with starting oral sex at a younger age, recognising that barrier methods reduce but do not eliminate risk. Avoid smoking, which independently increases the risk of HPV-related cancers and appears to make it harder for the body to clear persistent infection. Take unexplained, persistent throat or neck symptoms seriously and seek medical evaluation, since there is no routine screening test to catch HPV-related throat cancer early the way a Pap smear can for cervical cancer. A shared virus deserves a shared conversation Cervical cancer and HPV-related throat cancer are often discussed as though they belong to entirely separate conversations, one about women's reproductive health, the other barely discussed at all. But they are driven by the same virus, using the same molecular playbook, and they respond to the same core prevention tools: vaccination, informed sexual health choices, and not smoking. As Ghana pushes forward with its HPV vaccination campaign, broadening the public conversation to include throat cancer, and to include boys and men, could close a gap in awareness before it becomes a gap in survival. analysis.location_and_population: Ghana (nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for girls aged 9–14); United States (behavioral and epidemiological studies on oral HPV and oropharyngeal cancer); global context for HPV-associated cancers.
analysis.event: A media feature explaining how high-risk HPV types (especially HPV-16 and HPV-18) cause both cervical and oropharyngeal cancers through shared molecular mechanisms (E6/E7 proteins), with emphasis on oral sex as a transmission route to the throat. analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV causes the majority of cervical cancers and a large share of oropharyngeal cancers worldwide; HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection globally; HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers have risen sharply in higher-income countries; Ghana records over 117,000 new cervical cancer cases and 76,000 deaths annually; men are roughly six times more likely than women to carry oncogenic oral HPV; dose-response relationship between number of oral-sex partners and risk of HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Ghana launched a nationwide HPV vaccination campaign in October 2025 targeting 2.4 million girls aged 9–14, aiming to prevent tens of thousands of future cervical cancer deaths and align with WHO’s elimination target; no routine screening test exists for HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer; symptoms (persistent sore throat, difficulty swallowing, neck lump, unresolved ear pain) often appear late; condoms reduce but do not eliminate HPV transmission risk.

analysis.brief_en: A feature in Modern Ghana explains how high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types—especially HPV-16 and HPV-18—drive both cervical and oropharyngeal cancers through the same molecular hijacking of host cell checkpoints (E6/E7 proteins). Oral sex is identified as the specific route that delivers HPV to the throat, with large U.S. studies showing a clear dose-response: people with more than ten lifetime oral-sex partners have over four times the odds of HPV-related throat cancer, and starting oral sex before age 18 or with older partners further raises risk. Globally, HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection and the leading cause of cervical cancer, while HPV-positive throat cancers have surged in higher-income countries. In Ghana, the article highlights the October 2025 launch of a nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 2.4 million girls aged 9–14, part of efforts to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem.

boys born in 2014 1st vaccination of this summer vacation 2nd vaccination before entering middle school Adolescents and adults should also be vaccinated 사진 확대 "It's not another disease, it's a vaccine that prevents cancer." It's frustrating that the vaccination rate is less than 20% even though the country is vaccinated for free. We need to complete the first dose this summer vacation so that we can complete the second dose before entering middle school." National vaccination (NIP) for human papillomavirus (HPV), which had been only applied to women, has been expanded to male adolescents since this year. Three months have passed since the scope of support has been expanded to 12-year-old boys, but the vaccination rate is insignificant. According to the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the 11th, as of the 26th of last month, the first HPV vaccination rate of boys born in 2014 was only 19.4%. Ha Jung-hoon, the author of Korea's representative parenting guide "Pipopppop119 Pediatrics," and Ha Jung-hoon, the director of Pediatrics, who has been in the clinical field for more than 30 years, is a mentor to Korean parents. Director Ha responded to the Mail Business interview, saying, "It is regrettable that we are experiencing the best period of vaccination." Director Ha said, "Because immune responses are active in adolescence, the more you get vaccinated at this time, the higher the prevention effect and longer it lasts," adding, "The currently approved tetravalent vaccine can prevent about 70% of cervical cancer and up to 97% of 9-valent vaccines." The problem is that there are still many people who misunderstand the HPV vaccine as a 'cervical cancer vaccine' and do not vaccinate it. In the early stages of its introduction, the emphasis on women-centered disease prevention data widened the gap in inoculation rates between men and women. Director Ha said, "The HPV vaccination rate for girls exceeds 90%, but the number of boys has been in single digits for several years. In most developed countries, the male and female vaccination rate remains equal." Prevention is more important as men are also not free from the risk of HPV infection and the incidence of related diseases is increasing. The number of male HPV reports increased by 83% from 117 in 2020 to 214 in 2024, according to the KDCA. In particular, the number of male patients in Korea was 45,586 as of last year, about five times that of women. "Since the NIP registration, the number of male adolescents has gradually increased, but it is not yet sufficient," Director Ha said. "All vaccinations are important, but the HPV vaccine is especially meaningful in that it can reduce the enormous burden of medical expenses related to cancer." In order to increase the vaccination rate of male adolescents, it is necessary to actively utilize simultaneous vaccination with other vaccines. Director Ha said, "In adolescence, parents don't visit hospitals often, unlike in infants and toddlers, so it is efficient to take the vaccine they need when they visit the hospital," adding, "If a boy's NIP age group is lowered by one year, it can be combined with simultaneous vaccination with tetanus, diphtheria, and Baekilhae (Tdap) vaccines, which are mainly for 11-year-olds." Adolescents and adults over the age of 13 who are not eligible for NIP support must also be vaccinated to catch up. Director Ha said, "The key to HPV vaccines is to get them before infection, and even after the NIP age, if they are before exposure to the virus, the vaccination value is high," adding, "Women need to get them before the age of 45 and men need to get them before the age of 26." He also expressed the opinion that the government should convert the NIP-supported vaccine from 4 to 9 in the future. The 9-valent vaccine can prevent five more high-risk viruses compared to tetravalent. Ha said, "Most Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries, as well as countries that are less financially comfortable than us, support the 9-valent vaccine. There is no reason not to be medically hit by 9," he said. From a public health perspective, male vaccination is also essential. If only women are vaccinated, an inoculation rate of 80-90% is required to form herd immunity, but if men and women are vaccinated together, it can be 60-70%. "The HPV vaccine has been vaccinated more than 500 million worldwide and is sufficiently proven to be introduced by 37 out of 38 OECD countries," Ha said. "The safety of the vaccine should be considered together with scientific statistics and risks when not inoculated, not individual papers, cases, or rumors." <Terminology> Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine Vaccines that block anal cancer, head and neck cancer, and genital warts (difficulty), which occur in both men and women, including cervical cancer in women. It's frustrating that the vaccination rate is less than 20% even though the country is vaccinated for free. We need to complete the first dose this summer vacation so that we can complete the second dose before entering middle school." National vaccination (NIP) for human papillomavirus (HPV), which had been only applied to women, has been expanded to male adolescents since this year. Three months have passed since the scope of support has been expanded to 12-year-old boys, but the vaccination rate is insignificant. According to the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the 11th, as of the 26th of last month, the first HPV vaccination rate of boys born in 2014 was only 19.4%. Ha Jung-hoon, the author of Korea's representative parenting guide "Pipopppop119 Pediatrics," and Ha Jung-hoon, the director of Pediatrics, who has been in the clinical field for more than 30 years, is a mentor to Korean parents. Director Ha responded to the Mail Business interview, saying, "It is regrettable that we are experiencing the best period of vaccination." Director Ha said, "Because immune responses are active in adolescence, the more you get vaccinated at this time, the higher the prevention effect and longer it lasts," adding, "The currently approved tetravalent vaccine can prevent about 70% of cervical cancer and up to 97% of 9-valent vaccines." The problem is that there are still many people who misunderstand the HPV vaccine as a 'cervical cancer vaccine' and do not vaccinate it. In the early stages of its introduction, the emphasis on women-centered disease prevention data widened the gap in inoculation rates between men and women. Director Ha said, "The HPV vaccination rate for girls exceeds 90%, but the number of boys has been in single digits for several years. In most developed countries, the male and female vaccination rate remains equal." Prevention is more important as men are also not free from the risk of HPV infection and the incidence of related diseases is increasing. The number of male HPV reports increased by 83% from 117 in 2020 to 214 in 2024, according to the KDCA. In particular, the number of male patients in Korea was 45,586 as of last year, about five times that of women. "Since the NIP registration, the number of male adolescents has gradually increased, but it is not yet sufficient," Director Ha said. "All vaccinations are important, but the HPV vaccine is especially meaningful in that it can reduce the enormous burden of medical expenses related to cancer." In order to increase the vaccination rate of male adolescents, it is necessary to actively utilize simultaneous vaccination with other vaccines. Director Ha said, "In adolescence, parents don't visit hospitals often, unlike in infants and toddlers, so it is efficient to take the vaccine they need when they visit the hospital," adding, "If a boy's NIP age group is lowered by one year, it can be combined with simultaneous vaccination with tetanus, diphtheria, and Baekilhae (Tdap) vaccines, which are mainly for 11-year-olds." Adolescents and adults over the age of 13 who are not eligible for NIP support must also be vaccinated to catch up. Director Ha said, "The key to HPV vaccines is to get them before infection, and even after the NIP age, if they are before exposure to the virus, the vaccination value is high," adding, "Women need to get them before the age of 45 and men need to get them before the age of 26." He also expressed the opinion that the government should convert the NIP-supported vaccine from 4 to 9 in the future. The 9-valent vaccine can prevent five more high-risk viruses compared to tetravalent. Ha said, "Most Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries, as well as countries that are less financially comfortable than us, support the 9-valent vaccine. There is no reason not to be medically hit by 9," he said. From a public health perspective, male vaccination is also essential. If only women are vaccinated, an inoculation rate of 80-90% is required to form herd immunity, but if men and women are vaccinated together, it can be 60-70%. "The HPV vaccine has been vaccinated more than 500 million worldwide and is sufficiently proven to be introduced by 37 out of 38 OECD countries," Ha said. "The safety of the vaccine should be considered together with scientific statistics and risks when not inoculated, not individual papers, cases, or rumors." <Terminology> Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine Vaccines that block anal cancer, head and neck cancer, and genital warts (difficulty), which occur in both men and women, including cervical cancer in women. VIDEOS UPenn Dental Research: Antiviral and Antibacterial Chewing Gum Targets HPV and Oral Pathogens Linked to Head and Neck Cancer 10 Aug UPenn Dental Research: Antiviral and Antibacterial Chewing Gum Targets HPV and Oral Pathogens Linked to Head and Neck Cancer Posted at 00:59h in Cancer Research, Dental Research, HPV by Marie Benz MD FAAD MedicalResearch.com Interview with: Henry Daniell, PhD Vice-Chair and W.D. Miller Professor Department of Basic & Translational Sciences School of Dental Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia PA Dr. Henry Daniell, Ph.D. MedicalResearch.com: What is the background for this study? What bacteria or viruses are associated with head and neck squamous cell carcinomas? Dr. Daniell: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV), anaerobic bacteria Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) correlate with worse survival of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). In tumorigenic cells HPV genome integrates into the host cell genome causing genome instability and genic alteration which facilitate mutation and hyperproliferation. One third of males in the globe is HPV positive and one fifth are infected with high risk HPV16 strain. Pg is invasive and replicates within tumor cells and influences oncogenic signaling of HNSCC. Fn triggers cancer progression by upregulating several oncogenes responsible for inflammation, cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis. Therefore, it is important to control HPV, Pg, and Fn in the oral cavity to reduce initiation or advancement of oral cancer. MedicalResearch.com: What are the main findings of chewing gum with Bean-lectin (FRIL) gum? Dr. Daniell: Antiviral action of FRIL — Flt3 Receptor Interacting Lectin (FRIL) present in lablab bean contains four carbohydrate-binding domains that bind efficiently to complex N-glycans present on virus surface, thereby entrapping virus into large aggregates thereby blocking viral entry into host cells. In addition, FRIL blocks viruses at the endosome level in host cells upon entry. In our Ex vivo clinical study, Bean-lectin (FRIL) gum single treatment (trapped) aggregated 93% of HPV in saliva and 80% in oral-rinse samples from HNSCC patients. Higher aggregation is saliva is due to higher viral load in saliva than oral rinse samples. However, in our clinical trial, we will evaluate three gums per day for four weeks duration to evaluate changes in HPV viral load. MedicalResearch.com: Does the gum affect any other oral or gastrointestinal organisms, i.e. Helicobacter pylori? Dr. Daniell: Our antibacterial chewing gum contains the antimicrobial peptide protegrin. In Ex vivo clinical studies, single dose of bean gum + protegrin-1 reduced Pg/Fn > 99% in saliva and oral-rinse samples (n = 42). However, in our clinical trial, we will evaluate three gums per day for four weeks duration to evaluate changes in HPV viral load. Although protegrin was effective against anaerobic Pg/Fn, it did not kill capsule forming bacteria including Streptococci, providing selectivity and protection of oral commensal bacteria. However, this selectivity is not a property of protegrin, but several oral bacteria protect themselves via capsules or biofilms. It is unlikely that gastrointestinal organisms will be affected because protegrin could be degraded by acids and enzymes in the stomach. MedicalResearch.com: What should readers take away from your report? Dr. Daniell: Very little attention is paid to oral cancer related oral microbiome. Current treatments focus on surgical removal of tumors followed by radiation or chemotherapy. These treatments damage salivary glands, reduce saliva production, cause oral mucositis, and increase abundance of Candida albicans. Therefore, it is important to evaluate antiviral chewing gum at the onset of HNSCC before lesions advance to tumors, antibacterial gum during oral mucositis and antifungal gum post-radiation therapy. For related context on how oral bacteria are linked to HNSCC risk, see this MedicalResearch.com interview on oral bacterial species linked to a 50% increased risk of developing head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. MedicalResearch.com: Is there anything else you would like to add? Any disclosures? Dr. Daniell: In addition to initiation of tumor, Pg, Fn and C. albicans secrete carcinogenic metabolites like acetaldehyde by converting glucose or alcohol. Therefore, elimination of these pathogenic microbes should help oral cancer patients at early stages of onset. While clinical trials are conducted in HNSCC or mucositis patients to evaluate safety and efficacy, antiviral/antibacterial/antifungal chewing gums could be used as prophylaxis to prevent infection by these pathogenic microbes. Disclosures: None disclosed. Citation: Daniell, H., Wakade, G., Singh, R. et al. Ex vivo HNSCC clinical studies using saliva and antiviral or antibacterial chewing gums reveal reduction in carcinogenic microbes. VIDEOS UPenn Dental Research: Antiviral and Antibacterial Chewing Gum Targets HPV and Oral Pathogens Linked to Head and Neck Cancer 10 Aug UPenn Dental Research: Antiviral and Antibacterial Chewing Gum Targets HPV and Oral Pathogens Linked to Head and Neck Cancer Posted at 00:59h in Cancer Research, Dental Research, HPV by Marie Benz MD FAAD MedicalResearch.com Interview with: Henry Daniell, PhD Vice-Chair and W.D. Miller Professor Department of Basic & Translational Sciences School of Dental Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia PA Dr. Henry Daniell, Ph.D. MedicalResearch.com: What is the background for this study? What bacteria or viruses are associated with head and neck squamous cell carcinomas? Dr. Daniell: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV), anaerobic bacteria Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) correlate with worse survival of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). In tumorigenic cells HPV genome integrates into the host cell genome causing genome instability and genic alteration which facilitate mutation and hyperproliferation. One third of males in the globe is HPV positive and one fifth are infected with high risk HPV16 strain. Pg is invasive and replicates within tumor cells and influences oncogenic signaling of HNSCC. Fn triggers cancer progression by upregulating several oncogenes responsible for inflammation, cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis. Therefore, it is important to control HPV, Pg, and Fn in the oral cavity to reduce initiation or advancement of oral cancer. MedicalResearch.com: What are the main findings of chewing gum with Bean-lectin (FRIL) gum? Dr. Daniell: Antiviral action of FRIL — Flt3 Receptor Interacting Lectin (FRIL) present in lablab bean contains four carbohydrate-binding domains that bind efficiently to complex N-glycans present on virus surface, thereby entrapping virus into large aggregates thereby blocking viral entry into host cells. In addition, FRIL blocks viruses at the endosome level in host cells upon entry. In our Ex vivo clinical study, Bean-lectin (FRIL) gum single treatment (trapped) aggregated 93% of HPV in saliva and 80% in oral-rinse samples from HNSCC patients. Higher aggregation is saliva is due to higher viral load in saliva than oral rinse samples. However, in our clinical trial, we will evaluate three gums per day for four weeks duration to evaluate changes in HPV viral load. MedicalResearch.com: Does the gum affect any other oral or gastrointestinal organisms, i.e. Helicobacter pylori? Dr. Daniell: Our antibacterial chewing gum contains the antimicrobial peptide protegrin. In Ex vivo clinical studies, single dose of bean gum + protegrin-1 reduced Pg/Fn > 99% in saliva and oral-rinse samples (n = 42). However, in our clinical trial, we will evaluate three gums per day for four weeks duration to evaluate changes in HPV viral load. Although protegrin was effective against anaerobic Pg/Fn, it did not kill capsule forming bacteria including Streptococci, providing selectivity and protection of oral commensal bacteria. However, this selectivity is not a property of protegrin, but several oral bacteria protect themselves via capsules or biofilms. It is unlikely that gastrointestinal organisms will be affected because protegrin could be degraded by acids and enzymes in the stomach. MedicalResearch.com: What should readers take away from your report? Dr. Daniell: Very little attention is paid to oral cancer related oral microbiome. Current treatments focus on surgical removal of tumors followed by radiation or chemotherapy. These treatments damage salivary glands, reduce saliva production, cause oral mucositis, and increase abundance of Candida albicans. Therefore, it is important to evaluate antiviral chewing gum at the onset of HNSCC before lesions advance to tumors, antibacterial gum during oral mucositis and antifungal gum post-radiation therapy. For related context on how oral bacteria are linked to HNSCC risk, see this MedicalResearch.com interview on oral bacterial species linked to a 50% increased risk of developing head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. MedicalResearch.com: Is there anything else you would like to add? Any disclosures? Dr. Daniell: In addition to initiation of tumor, Pg, Fn and C. albicans secrete carcinogenic metabolites like acetaldehyde by converting glucose or alcohol. Therefore, elimination of these pathogenic microbes should help oral cancer patients at early stages of onset. While clinical trials are conducted in HNSCC or mucositis patients to evaluate safety and efficacy, antiviral/antibacterial/antifungal chewing gums could be used as prophylaxis to prevent infection by these pathogenic microbes. news.content_zh: 宾夕法尼亚大学牙科医学院的研究人员开发了一种 抗病毒药物 和抗菌口香糖,旨在减少高危 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 以及口腔病原体牙龈卟啉单胞菌和具核梭杆菌,这些病原体与头颈鳞状细胞癌 (HNSCC) 有关。在离体临床研究中,单个 治疗 聚集了 HNSCC 患者唾液中 93% 的 HPV 和口腔冲洗样本中 80% 的 HPV,而抗菌成分则使唾液和口腔冲洗样本中的牙龈卟啉单胞菌和具核梭菌减少了 99% 以上 (n=42)。研究小组计划进行一项临床试验,评估每天三块牙龈,持续四个星期,以测量 HPV 病毒载量的变化。这种口香糖选择性地针对病原微生物,而不伤害口腔共生体或胃肠道微生物,为预防 HPV 相关的 HNSCC 进展提供了一种潜在的预防方法。

news.content: Skip to content August 15, 2026 1:37 am हिन्दी தமிழ் Languages English हिन्दी தமிழ் English हिन्दी தமிழ் Login No products in the cart. ₹0.00 0 Cart Daily Current Affairs International National Economy Science Technology Defence Appointments Sports Environment Daily Current Affairs International National Economy Science Technology Defence Appointments Sports Environment UPSC Current Affairs SSC Current Affairs RRB Current Affairs Banking Current Affairs TNPSC Current Affairs UPSC Current Affairs SSC Current Affairs RRB Current Affairs Banking Current Affairs TNPSC Current Affairs Home - Science Technology India Validates Indigenous HPV Test for Affordable Cervical Cancer Screening Updated - June 11, 2026 10:40 am CURRENT AFFAIRS: Truenat HR-HPV-Plus, AIIMS New Delhi, ICMR, Cervical Cancer Screening, Human Papillomavirus, IARC, Molbio Diagnostics, Women’s Health, WHO Standards, Public Health Full Article One Liner Quiz Mode CA PDF Indigenous HPV Test Receives International Validation India Validates Indigenous HPV Test for Affordable Cervical Cancer Screening: Researchers from AIIMS New Delhi, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), France have successfully validated an indigenous Human Papillomavirus (HPV) test for cervical cancer screening. The validated test, Truenat HR-HPV-Plus, meets international performance standards and is expected to provide an affordable and accessible screening solution for women across India, especially those above 30 years of age. Static GK fact: AIIMS New Delhi was established in 1956 under the All India Institute of Medical Sciences Act, 1956, and functions under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Why HPV Screening Remains Essential HPV infection is the leading cause of cervical cancer, one of the most common cancers affecting women worldwide. Although HPV vaccination helps prevent future infections, regular screening remains essential for early detection of precancerous changes. Experts recommend HPV screening for women aged 30 years and above, as early diagnosis significantly improves treatment outcomes and reduces mortality. Static GK Tip: Cervical cancer develops in the cervix and is primarily caused by persistent infection with high-risk HPV types. Features of Truenat HR-HPV-Plus Among four indigenous HPV DNA tests evaluated, Truenat HR-HPV-Plus, developed by Molbio Diagnostics, was the only test to satisfy all international validation criteria established by WHO and IARC. The test detects eight high-risk HPV types responsible for nearly 95% of cervical cancer cases. It also demonstrated high accuracy, reliable reproducibility across laboratories, and suitability for use in district and sub-district healthcare facilities. Static GK fact: Molbio Diagnostics is an Indian biotechnology company known for developing the Truenat molecular diagnostic platform. Validation Study and Public Health Significance The validation study was supported by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) under the Grand Challenges India initiative. Researchers evaluated four Indian-developed HPV tests using 1,159 cervical samples, including confirmed precancerous lesions and cervical cancer cases. The study followed internationally accepted WHO and IARC validation benchmarks. Static GK Tip: BIRAC is a not-for-profit public sector enterprise under the Department of Biotechnology, promoting innovation in biotechnology and healthcare. Impact on India’s Healthcare System The validated indigenous test is expected to reduce India’s dependence on imported HPV screening technologies and lower the cost of large-scale cervical cancer screening. Its compatibility with the existing Truenat diagnostic infrastructure will enable rapid deployment in rural and semi-urban healthcare centres, improving access to early detection and supporting India’s efforts to reduce cervical cancer burden. Why HPV Screening Remains Essential HPV infection is the leading cause of cervical cancer, one of the most common cancers affecting women worldwide.
