Sibel Elif Gülteki̇n1 Show authors 27 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Sialadenoma papilliferum (SP) is a rare benign salivary gland tumor characterized by a distinctive biphasic architecture and clinical resemblance to other papillary lesions of the oral cavity. Although recent studies have identified alterations in the MAPK pathway, particularly BRAF V600E mutations, the molecular landscape of this rare lesion remains incompletely characterized. We report a case of SP arising in the floor of the mouth of a 25-year-old male patient. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of SP, while immunohistochemical analysis revealed p63 positivity and negative staining for BRAF V600E and p16. Molecular analysis detected HPV-11 DNA by PCR-RFLP. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first reported case of HPV-11 DNA detection in SP. Further studies are needed to clarify the biological significance of HPV detection and to better characterize the molecular pathways involved in the development of this rare lesion. Sibel Elif Gülteki̇n1 Show authors 27 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Sialadenoma papilliferum (SP) is a rare benign salivary gland tumor characterized by a distinctive biphasic architecture and clinical resemblance to other papillary lesions of the oral cavity. Although recent studies have identified alterations in the MAPK pathway, particularly BRAF V600E mutations, the molecular landscape of this rare lesion remains incompletely characterized. We report a case of SP arising in the floor of the mouth of a 25-year-old male patient. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of SP, while immunohistochemical analysis revealed p63 positivity and negative staining for BRAF V600E and p16. Molecular analysis detected HPV-11 DNA by PCR-RFLP. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first reported case of HPV-11 DNA detection in SP. Further studies are needed to clarify the biological significance of HPV detection and to better characterize the molecular pathways involved in the development of this rare lesion. news.content: Express Healthcare Close the sidebar Express Healthcare Beyond Cervical cancer: Why HPV-related head and neck cancers need greater attention Dr Janaki MG, Senior Consultant – Radiation Oncology, Ramaiah Institute of Oncosciences, Ramaiah Memorial Hospital, discusses the evolving role of HPV in head and neck cancers, the gaps in India’s current approach and why prevention, including wider HPV vaccination, needs greater attention By Dr Janaki MG on August 12, 2026 Globally, Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) related head and neck cancers have surged by more than 225 per cent over the past 50 years, even as tobacco- and alcohol-driven cases have declined in many developed nations, according to a GLOBOCAN-based analysisi. In India, a systematic review and meta-analysis of over 4,600 head and neck cancer patients found the overall pooled HPV prevalence to be 33 per cent with striking regional variation, ranging from 47 percent in Eastern India to under 20 percent in Western Indiaii. HPV is responsible for nearly all cervical cancer cases while an emerging and often under-appreciated dimension of HPV-related disease is its growing role in head and neck cancers, particularly cancers of the oropharynx (the tonsils and base of the tongue). A changing disease landscape Head and neck cancers in India have traditionally been linked to tobacco and alcohol use, with a consistent patient profile of older individuals, often with a long history of chewing tobacco, smoking, or heavy drinking. Over the past decade, however, there is a distinct shift. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers are being diagnosed at younger ages, with different sexual practices and multiple sexual partners. The disease biology is quite different from that of its tobacco-related counterpart in terms of better response to radiation and chemotherapy. Many HPV-positive patients also have concurrent tobacco or alcohol habits, suggesting dual risk factors rather than a clean substitution of one cause for another. What remains consistent, though, is the clinical relevance of HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers that tends to respond better to treatment and carry a markedly better prognosis, 5-year survival rates exceeding 80 percent in HPV-positive cases, compared to under 50 percent in HPV-negative disease. Why it matters for India India already carries one of the world’s highest burdens of head and neck cancers, driven largely by tobacco use. In addition HPV positivity is increasing in India over time and its very important to prevent further rise. Layered onto this is a meaningful and measurable HPV contribution, one that gets more complicated when you look closer at the regional picture. A meta-analysis published in BMC Infectious Diseases found that HPV prevalence in head and neck cancers in Eastern India runs nearly 2.5 times higher than in the Westiii. This probably corresponds to higher occurrence of head and neck cancers in the east. It points to something we still don’t fully understand HPV’s role in Indian head and neck cancers isn’t uniform, and our current data is too fragmented to tell us why. This information helps us to identify the areas where we need to focus regarding early diagnosis and prevention. Bridging the gaps Closing this gap isn’t about one intervention, it requires movement on several fronts at once: A patient with a persistent sore throat, an unexplained lump in the neck, or something unusual in the tonsils shouldn’t be dismissed simply because they don’t fit the “typical” head and neck cancer profile, particularly in regions where we already know HPV prevalence runs high. HPV testing, where clinically appropriate, should be integrated into diagnostic workups for oropharyngeal cancers, helping both with prognostication and treatment planning. Clinician awareness needs deliberate reinforcement. Many primary care physicians and even some specialists continue to associate HPV almost exclusively with gynaecological disease. Continuing medical education must catch up with the evolving evidence base. Multidisciplinary care pathways, involving oncologists, ENT surgeons, radiation oncologists, and pathologists are essential to ensure that once identified, HPV-positive cases are managed with an approach suited to their distinct biology and prognosis, while accounting for the dual-risk-factor reality common in Indian patients. Prevention beyond cervical cancer Reframing HPV vaccination as a broader cancer prevention strategy, rather than a gender-specific intervention, could meaningfully expand its public health impact and address a population at risk that current campaigns largely not covering. The way forward As India continues its efforts against viral and vaccine-preventable diseases, HPV-related head and neck cancers deserve further research in terms of actual assessment of the existing regional burden identification, dedicated research into better understanding of the strains involved, wider vaccination efforts and analysis of the outcome of treatment of HPV associated oropharyngeal cancers. Unlike cervical cancer where time tested screening methods are available, screening for these cancers are difficult and hence prevention should be of topmost priority. Vaccination schedules are similar to that for cervical cancer and requires to be implemented across the country especially for high risk susceptible population. analysis.location_and_population: India; national scope with regional variation (Eastern India vs Western India); affected population includes head and neck cancer patients and clinicians.
analysis.event: A commentary by a senior radiation oncologist highlights the rising burden and distinct epidemiology of HPV-related head and neck cancers in India, emphasizing gaps in prevention, diagnosis, and clinician awareness.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Globally, HPV-related head and neck cancers have increased by more than 225% over the past 50 years; in India, pooled HPV prevalence in head and neck cancers is 33% with regional variation (47% in Eastern India, under 20% in Western India); HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers show better prognosis (5-year survival >80%) than HPV-negative cases (<50%).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Calls for integrating HPV testing into diagnostic workups for oropharyngeal cancers, strengthening clinician education, adopting multidisciplinary care pathways, and expanding HPV vaccination beyond cervical cancer prevention; regional burden remains insufficiently characterized and research gaps persist.

analysis.brief_en: A senior Indian oncologist warns that HPV-related head and neck cancers are surging globally and in India, where they now account for a third of cases but with sharp regional differences—reaching nearly half of patients in the east versus under one-fifth in the west. Unlike tobacco-linked tumors, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers strike younger adults and respond far better to treatment, yet many clinicians still overlook HPV outside gynecologic disease. The commentary urges wider HPV vaccination, routine HPV testing in oropharyngeal cancer workups, and targeted prevention in high-burden regions, noting that current data remain fragmented and that screening for these cancers is difficult.

news.title_original: 万泰生物:九价HPV疫苗泰国获批 实现首份境外上市许可 - 东方财富

analysis.time: The article was published on 2026-08-11 (18:21 local time). The company’s announcement and the Thai Food and Drug Administration’s approval were both reported on the evening of 11 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The approval was granted by Thailand’s Food and Drug Administration for a vaccine developed by China’s Wan‐Tai Biotech (Xiamen Wan‐Tai Canghai Biotech Co.). The nine‐valent HPV vaccine is intended for females aged 9‐45 years.
analysis.event: Wan‐Tai Biotech announced that its domestically‐developed nine‐valent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine received regulatory approval from the Thai FDA, marking the first overseas marketing licence for the product. The information comes from the company’s official notice and is reported by China Securities Journal via Eastmoney.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No case or death numbers are reported. The approval enables export of the vaccine to Thailand, expanding Wan‐Tai’s market presence in Southeast Asia and potentially preventing infections from HPV types 16/18/31/33/45/52/58 and 6/11 in the target female population. No specific risk statements are provided.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Regulatory review in Thailand is complete; the vaccine is now authorized for commercial distribution there. The company plans to use the licence to launch sales and further expand into other Southeast Asian markets. No outstanding uncertainties are mentioned in the source.

analysis.brief_en: Wan‐Tai Biotech’s wholly‐owned subsidiary announced on 11 August 2026 that its nine‐valent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine has received approval from Thailand’s Food and Drug Administration, securing the first overseas marketing licence for the product. The vaccine, developed in China, targets females aged 9‐45 and covers high‐risk HPV types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 as well as low‐risk types 6 and 11. The regulatory clearance enables Wan‐Tai to export the vaccine to Thailand and lays the groundwork for broader expansion across Southeast Asia, potentially reducing HPV‐related disease burden in the region. No case numbers, deaths, or safety concerns were reported, and the approval process is described as complete with no remaining uncertainties.

MEDINDIA MEDINDIA Consult Online Doctor Courses Explore Healthy Living News Health A-Z Calculators Articles Drugs Directories Education More Search Medindia Medindia » News » Health In Focus » Why HPV Vaccination Matters for Boys as Well as Girls Why HPV Vaccination Matters for Boys as Well as Girls Written by Dr. Vasantha Medically Reviewed by Colleen Fleiss M.Sc on Aug 14 2026 3:20 PM HPV vaccination may have a broader role in protecting boys and young men from certain HPV-related cancers. Highlights: HPV vaccination was linked to a lower risk of HPV-related cancers in males Male cancer prevention gains importance as HPV vaccination benefits extend beyond cervical cancer HPV-related cancers studied included head and neck, esophageal, anal and penile cancers HPV vaccination is often discussed in connection with cervical cancer, but a new finding highlights why the vaccine also matters for boys and young men. A study is shifting the conversation from HPV vaccination as a women’s health measure to broader cancer prevention for both sexes (1✔ ✔Trusted Source Nine-Valent Human Papillomavirus Vaccination and Related Cancers in Males Go to source). A study published in JAMA Oncology found that vaccination was linked to a lower risk of several HPV-related cancers in males. The analysis included 615,155 vaccinated males and 2,290,623 unvaccinated males aged 9 to 26 years. After matching the groups, more than 510,000 males were included in each group, with outcomes followed for up to 10 years. The vaccinated group had a 46% lower risk of the combined HPV-related cancer outcome. Human Papillomavirus Infection - Risk Factors, Symptoms, Screening, Treatment & Prevention Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, depending on the human papillomavirus that causes it, can result in common warts or can cause cervical cancer. HPV Vaccination And Cancer Risk In Males The researchers looked at cancers linked to HPV in four areas: Head and neck Esophagus Anus Penis For someone deciding whether an adolescent boy should receive the 9-valent HPV vaccine, the findings add evidence that the potential benefits extend beyond the health concerns traditionally associated with girls and women. The study did not find that vaccination eliminates cancer risk. Instead, it found an association between vaccination and lower cancer incidence, making the distinction important when interpreting the findings. HPV Infection : Two-Dose Vaccine Found Effective In Treating Genital Warts Genital warts occur as a result of Human Papillomavirus infections. Two doses of HPV vaccine could be effective in treating genital warts. HPV Vaccine Benefits For Boys And Young Men The lower cancer incidence was seen among both younger males aged 9 to 14 years and those aged 15 to 26 years. This suggests that the observed association was not limited to one age group within the population studied. For a family discussing routine healthcare for a school-age boy, HPV vaccination can therefore be viewed as part of a broader approach to protecting against HPV-related disease, rather than as a vaccine relevant only to girls. Test Your Knowledge on Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is the most common sexually transmitted infection spread by person to person contact, mainly sexual intercourse and affecting the skin and genital areas. There are over 100 types of HPV and some types can cause ... Why HPV Vaccination Matters Beyond Cervical Cancer HPV-related cancer can affect people irrespective of sex. The findings are particularly relevant because vaccination programmes have often been discussed through the lens of cervical cancer prevention. So, sex-neutral HPV vaccination can have relevance for male health as well. Therefore, "the 9v-HPV vaccine is beneficial not only for females but also for males," according to Taito Kitano and Sayaka Yoshida. Travel Vaccination Calculator Find out about travel shots or vaccination before you travel to your destination country. Travel vaccination calculator guides travelers on information about travel to 247 countries. Safe travel is the first step to enjoy your holiday or business ... What The HPV Vaccine Findings Mean For Families Consider a parent reviewing recommended vaccinations for a son during adolescence. The decision is no longer only about preventing an infection that may affect someone else later in life. The evidence indicates that vaccination may also be associated with a lower risk of certain cancers affecting males. The study also included young men aged 15 to 26 years. However, this observational evidence should be understood as an association rather than proof that vaccination directly caused the lower cancer risk. HPV Vaccination And Sex-Neutral Cancer Prevention The broader significance lies in how HPV vaccination is viewed. Cancer prevention is not exclusively a women's health issue, and the findings support considering HPV vaccination within a sex-neutral prevention strategy. The evidence does not establish protection against every HPV-related cancer or disease. It specifically examined the combined occurrence of head and neck, esophageal, anal and penile cancers among the male population studied. Going forward, these findings add support to a more inclusive understanding of HPV vaccination, where protecting boys and young men is also considered part of reducing the burden of HPV-related cancers. For families making vaccination decisions, understanding who can benefit from HPV prevention can make conversations with healthcare professionals more informed and meaningful. Frequently Asked Questions Q: What types of cancer were linked to HPV vaccination in males? A: The study examined four cancer groups associated with human papillomavirus (HPV): head and neck cancers, esophageal cancer, anal cancer and penile cancer. Researchers assessed whether males who received the 9-valent HPV vaccine had a different risk of developing these cancers compared with unvaccinated males. Q: Does the HPV vaccine reduce cancer risk in males? A: The study found an association between HPV vaccination and a lower risk of the combined HPV-related cancer outcome in males. This adds to evidence that HPV vaccination may provide important cancer-prevention benefits for males as well as females. However, an observational study showing an association does not by itself prove that vaccination directly caused the lower cancer risk. Q: Why is HPV vaccination important for boys and young men? A: HPV can infect both males and females and is associated with several cancers. Vaccinating boys and young men can help protect them against HPV infections that may later contribute to cancer. It can also contribute to broader HPV prevention by reducing transmission within the population. Q: At what age were males included in the HPV vaccine study? A: The study included males aged 9 to 26 years who had either received the 9-valent HPV vaccine or remained unvaccinated. Researchers compared cancer outcomes between the vaccinated and unvaccinated groups. Q: What is the 9-valent HPV vaccine? A: The 9-valent HPV vaccine protects against nine types of HPV that are associated with HPV-related diseases and cancers. It is designed to provide broader protection against HPV types than earlier HPV vaccines. Q: Does the HPV vaccine protect males against every type of cancer? A: No. HPV vaccination does not prevent every form of cancer. The study specifically examined head and neck, esophageal, anal and penile cancers in relation to HPV vaccination. The vaccine is intended to prevent infection with specific HPV types and, in turn, reduce the risk of diseases associated with those infections. Q: Can HPV cause cancer in men? A: Yes. HPV infection can contribute to several cancers in males, including anal, penile and certain head and neck cancers. Most HPV infections do not lead to cancer, but persistent infection with certain high-risk HPV types can cause cellular changes that may eventually become cancerous. Q: Does HPV vaccination work only when given before HPV exposure? A: HPV vaccines work best when administered before exposure to HPV, which is why vaccination is recommended at younger ages. The vaccine prevents new HPV infections but does not treat an HPV infection or cancer that is already present. Q: Does this study prove that HPV vaccination prevents cancer in males? A: The findings provide evidence of a lower observed risk of the combined HPV-related cancer outcome among vaccinated males, but the study design should be considered when interpreting the results. An association between vaccination and lower cancer incidence does not necessarily establish direct causation on its own. Q: Should parents consider HPV vaccination for boys? A: The findings add to the evidence supporting HPV vaccination for males, particularly because HPV can cause cancers in men as well as women. Parents should discuss the appropriate vaccination schedule and individual circumstances with a qualified healthcare professional. news.content_title: Costs of Surveillance Care After Definitive Treatment of Head and Neck Cancer: A Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-Medicare Analysis
news.content: Abstract Introduction: Following curative treatment of squamous carcinoma of the head and neck, surveillance care is indicated to detect recurrence. Historically, physical exams are the backbone of surveillance, but serial imaging and flexible endoscopy are also utilized. Recently, assays have become commercially available, which could aid in early detection of recurrence. To understand the potential economic impact of these assays, a baseline of surveillance costs must be established. We performed a Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-Medicare analysis to quantify the costs of classic surveillance procedures. Materials and methods: We obtained data from the 2010-2017 SEER program linked to traditional Medicare Part A & B claims and enrollment information dating 2010-2019. Patients with non-metastatic cancers of the head and neck, including oral cavity, paranasal sinus, pharynx, and larynx, were identified. Definitive treatment with either surgery or radiation therapy (with or without systemic therapy) was required for inclusion. Patients were excluded if they had any lapse in insurance coverage (i.e., Parts A & B) or were enrolled in Medicare Advantage. The surveillance period was defined from 90 days past treatment through the date of death, hospice enrollment, or additional cancer treatments. Procedures related to routine surveillance were identified, including flexible endoscopy and imaging. The cumulative Medicare spend was quantified, adjusting for inflation to 2021 U.S. dollars. Results: In total, 13,339 patients were identified; all were age ≥ 65. The most common site was the oropharynx (OPC), followed by larynx cancers. Of the OPC patients, 33% were human papillomavirus positive (HPV+), and for 55%, the HPV status was unknown. The median clinical follow-up was 43.0 months, and the median surveillance period was 16.6 months. The median costs were $1,246 (IQR $420-$2,381), with the top 5% incurring a cost of $7,657 (IQR $6,656-9,062). Surveillance was more expensive among younger, HPV+ OPC patients and for those who followed longer. Flexible laryngoscopy was the most frequent charge. Conclusions: In an older population, payer costs follow a wide and skewed distribution but are highest among younger HPV+ OPC patients. These findings facilitate cost-effectiveness assessment of novel assays. Opportunity exists to reduce imaging and endoscopy spend by substituting more accurate biomarkers. Introduction Head and neck cancer (HNC) presents a significant global health concern, accounting for over 790,000 new cases annually [1]. Despite therapeutic advances, recurrence rates remain high: up to 40% of patients experience disease recurrence after definitive treatment [2, 3]. Recurrence risk is highest in the initial post-treatment period and is influenced by factors such as tumor stage, human papillomavirus (HPV) status, and primary site [4]. Current surveillance strategies for HNC survivors are guided by consensus recommendations from organizations such as the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), American Cancer Society (ACS), and the American College of Radiology (ACR), which advocate for regular history and physical examination, with imaging reserved for symptomatic patients or those with abnormal findings [5-8]. The recommended frequency of clinical follow-up is every one to three months in the first year, every two to six months in the second year, and less frequently thereafter. However, the utility of routine imaging in asymptomatic patients is increasingly questioned, as multiple studies have failed to demonstrate a survival benefit or improved salvage rates with scheduled imaging compared to clinical examination alone [2, 9-11]. Routine surveillance imaging may contribute to unnecessary financial burden, radiation exposure, and resource utilization without clear evidence of benefit. Therefore, recent guidelines suggest that surveillance should be individualized based on recurrence risk, with only higher-risk patients for whom the tumor site is difficult to visualize considered for serial imaging [5, 12]. Moving beyond serial imaging, emerging evidence now supports the use of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and tumor tissue-modified viral (TTMV)-DNA assays as highly sensitive and specific tools for the early detection of recurrence, particularly in HPV-driven oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) [13-15]. These assays can be performed serially and have demonstrated high positive and negative predictive values, often identifying recurrence months before clinical or radiologic detection [16]. While promising, concerns over the costs of serial measurement have slowed the adoption of these biomarkers [17]. Initial cost-effectiveness modeling suggests that strict adherence to biomarkers instead of imaging may be economically feasible [17, 18]. However, the validity of any cost-effectiveness model is contingent upon the baseline costs of the reference (traditional surveillance modalities), which have not been well quantified. Herein, we used the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-Medicare database to quantify the costs of surveillance care in the pre-biomarker era, providing a foundation for a value assessment of novel assays used in survivorship. This work was presented in digital poster format at the 2025 American Society of Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) meeting. Materials & Methods Data source Formed in 1973, the SEER program is a set of population-based registries that was expanded from 18 to 21 geographical areas in 2018 and covers approximately 35% of the United States population [19]. Through a de-identified process, approximately 96% of cancer cases held in the SEER database are linked to Medicare claims data, forming a relational database queryable for cost of care. For this study, files obtained included (1) SEER Cancer Data, Medicare Enrollment Master Beneficiary Summary File (MBSF); (3) Medicare Provider Analysis and Review (MEDPAR) file; (4) National Claims History (NCH) file; (5) Outpatient file; and (6) Hospice file. Atrium Health Institutional Review Board approval was waived, and a Data Use Agreement was executed. This report conforms to STrengthening the Reporting of OBservational studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for observational research [20]. Study cohort We obtained data from the 2010-2017 SEER program linked to traditional Medicare Part A & B claims and enrollment information dating from 2010-2019. Patients without a surveillance period were counted to have a payment of zero but left in the analysis to ensure an accurate denominator. Analysis of cost patterns examined payments by age, race, ethnicity, diagnosis year, cancer site, and HPV status. Additionally, analyses were performed to assess Medicare payments by HPV status for oropharyngeal cancers alone as well as by secondary cancer treatment (surgery and radiation), and year of surveillance care. Lastly, average frequency of payments for each HCPCS code (n>15) in the surveillance period was analyzed across all patients in the study population. The most common site was oropharynx (OPC), followed by larynx primaries. Of the OPC patients, 34% were known HPV positive (HPV+). The most common reasons for discontinuing surveillance were additional treatment or hospice enrollment. These costs varied widely and demonstrated a rightward skew, with the top 5% of patients incurring significantly higher costs (median $7,657, IQR $6,656-9,062). Male patients had slightly higher costs than female patients ($1,323 vs. $1,082). Finally, these parameters can be used to improve the accuracy of additional cost-effectiveness assessments, which may guide more efficient health policies in the future. Second, the rationale for each HCPCS charge is not available in the data, and some "overcounting" of scan charges is likely. Opportunity exists to reduce imaging and endoscopy spend by substituting more accurate biomarkers such as ctDNA, though this may increase Medicare expenses overall. However, if restricted to a higher-risk population, it may be possible to demonstrate the cost-effectiveness of serial biomarkers. news.title_zh: 头颈癌最终 监测 治疗后的 监测 护理费用:监测、监测 和最终结果 (SEER)-医疗保险分析 - cureus.com
news.source_body_en: A SEER-Medicare analysis published 10 August 2026 quantified routine surveillance costs for 13,339 U.S. Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 and older treated for non-metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma between 2010 and 2017. Median payer spending during surveillance was $1,246, but costs were skewed, with the top 5% exceeding $7,600. Surveillance was most expensive among younger patients with HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer and those followed longer. Flexible laryngoscopy accounted for the majority of charges. The study, presented at ASTRO 2025, establishes a baseline to evaluate whether emerging HPV-driven recurrence assays could reduce imaging and endoscopy spending by enabling earlier detection.

Health Effects, Risk Factors for Exposure, and More 3Microplastics in Bottled Water Are More Abundant Than Previously Thought SEE MORE News Trump Issues Order to Change the Childhood Vaccine Schedule — Here’s What Doctors Want Parents to Know Major medical groups say the executive order isn’t based on science and would leave children vulnerable to preventable illnesses. iStock By Korin Miller Published on August 11, 2026 Fact-Checked by Emily Kay Votruba Add us on Google President Donald Trump signed a controversial executive order Monday that makes major changes to childhood vaccinations in the United States. [1] The executive order recommends vaccines against 11 preventable diseases, instead of the 17 currently identified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The plan also calls for splitting up the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine (currently given as a single shot) into three separate vaccines, and stresses “shared decision-making” when considering immunizations like the flu shot. [1] Multiple major medical organizations and lawmakers have spoken out against the changes. “Altering a proven vaccination schedule without credible evidence risks weakening public confidence and putting children’s health at risk,” said Willie Underwood III, MD, MPH, the president of the American Medical Association, in a statement shared with Everyday Health. What the Executive Order Said The executive order split its vaccine recommendations into categories: Vaccines recommended for all children: Measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella (chicken pox) Recommended for “certain high-risk groups or populations”: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue Vaccines that should be given only with shared clinical decision-making: Hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza, and COVID-19. Shared clinical-decision making means the default is not to vaccinate, and parents have to specifically request these vaccines. [2] The order also recommends splitting the combined MMR vaccine into “three separate single-disease shots” — an option not currently available in the United States. “To the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits,” the order states. The order cites vaccine guidance from “peer nations” as part of the rationale for the changes, which Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, calls an “interesting” claim. “Peer nations, that the administration often cherry-picks, all use the MMR,” he says. One exception is Japan, he notes, which uses a measles-rubella vaccine and gives a mumps vaccine separately. [3] Finally, the order called on the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines to present plans to the president to “improve” vaccine research related to the sequence, safety, and timing of childhood vaccines. It stressed that states have “obligations to provide religious and medical exemptions from childhood and adolescent immunization requirements,” and threatens "appropriate action” if these are not granted. Ultimately, though, only the states have the authority to determine which vaccinations are required for school attendance, not the federal government, notes Dr. Adalja. Trump Offers Disproven Autism Link as Rationale for Changes Although it was not mentioned in the executive order itself, President Trump repeatedly suggested in a press conference that childhood vaccines and their timing could play a role in rising autism rates — a claim disproven by decades of research. [4] “Dozens of studies involving millions of people show there is no link between vaccines and autism, and yet federal leaders continue to promote this outdated, disproven idea to scare families,” said Andrew D. Racine, MD, PhD, the president of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), in a statement. [5] “Today’s executive order will do nothing to support families of children with autism or advance understanding of the condition,” he added. AAP said it will not change its vaccine recommendations in response to the executive order. Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, issued his own statement on X. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” he wrote. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.” [6] Doctors Oppose the Recommendations for Many Reasons Experts say their biggest concern about the executive order is that it isn’t based on science. “We know that the current childhood vaccination schedule is supported by years of scientific evidence. These new recommendations are not,” says Jennifer M. Walsh, DNP, an assistant professor at George Washington University School of Nursing in Ashburn, Virginia, and a primary care pediatric nurse practitioner. As for dividing the MMR shot into three separate vaccines administered in separate medical visits, “Spacing them out doesn’t make any sense to reduce the burden on the immune system,” Walsh says. She points out that time spent on the playground can expose children to more antigens (substances that can trigger an immune response) than vaccination does. Besides, the combination shot is safe, Adalja says. “The combined shot exists because giving three antigens at once is exactly as safe as giving them separately,” he says. The changes would pose logistical and cost issues for families, too, Walsh says. “Spacing vaccines out leads to more incomplete vaccinations for kids,” she says. “It’s also a higher cost, and more of a burden on parents and healthcare practices because you have to have the staff come in for those multiple visits.” Parents will have to take more time off from work for all those vaccination visits, which can lead to a drop in earnings, and they may need to take additional time off if their child develops a fever or other reaction to the vaccines, she says. Other countries may also have different childhood vaccination schedules for a reason, Walsh adds. “They are different countries with different healthcare access and infrastructure,” she says. “It is not comparing apples to apples.” Order Unlikely to Impact Health Insurance Coverage Health insurers follow recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) when deciding on coverage, Adalja notes, and these guidelines predate the Trump administration. As a result, the executive order “will not have any impact on insurance coverage.” Consult With Your Healthcare Provider, Experts Say Walsh stresses the importance of getting vaccination advice from medical providers, not politicians. “Talk to your pediatric provider about vaccine recommendations,” she says. “We want to talk to parents about any concerns they have. It is our life mission to educate about why we do this, and to help kids thrive.” Adalja also recommends talking to your healthcare provider. “Follow the schedule your pediatrician and the American Academy of Pediatrics still publish independently of this order — that’s the one built from data, rather than politics,” he says. Racine, MD, PhD, the president of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), in a statement. [5] “Today’s executive order will do nothing to support families of children with autism or advance understanding of the condition,” he added. AAP said it will not change its vaccine recommendations in response to the executive order. Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, issued his own statement on X. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” he wrote. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.” [6] Doctors Oppose the Recommendations for Many Reasons Experts say their biggest concern about the executive order is that it isn’t based on science. “We know that the current childhood vaccination schedule is supported by years of scientific evidence. These new recommendations are not,” says Jennifer M. Walsh, DNP, an assistant professor at George Washington University School of Nursing in Ashburn, Virginia, and a primary care pediatric nurse practitioner. As for dividing the MMR shot into three separate vaccines administered in separate medical visits, “Spacing them out doesn’t make any sense to reduce the burden on the immune system,” Walsh says. She points out that time spent on the playground can expose children to more antigens (substances that can trigger an immune response) than vaccination does. Besides, the combination shot is safe, Adalja says. “The combined shot exists because giving three antigens at once is exactly as safe as giving them separately,” he says. The changes would pose logistical and cost issues for families, too, Walsh says. “Spacing vaccines out leads to more incomplete vaccinations for kids,” she says. “It’s also a higher cost, and more of a burden on parents and healthcare practices because you have to have the staff come in for those multiple visits.” Parents will have to take more time off from work for all those vaccination visits, which can lead to a drop in earnings, and they may need to take additional time off if their child develops a fever or other reaction to the vaccines, she says. Other countries may also have different childhood vaccination schedules for a reason, Walsh adds. “They are different countries with different healthcare access and infrastructure,” she says. “It is not comparing apples to apples.” Order Unlikely to Impact Health Insurance Coverage Health insurers follow recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) when deciding on coverage, Adalja notes, and these guidelines predate the Trump administration. As a result, the executive order “will not have any impact on insurance coverage.” Consult With Your Healthcare Provider, Experts Say Walsh stresses the importance of getting vaccination advice from medical providers, not politicians. “Talk to your pediatric provider about vaccine recommendations,” she says. “We want to talk to parents about any concerns they have. It is our life mission to educate about why we do this, and to help kids thrive.” Adalja also recommends talking to your healthcare provider. “Follow the schedule your pediatrician and the American Academy of Pediatrics still publish independently of this order — that’s the one built from data, rather than politics,” he says. analysis.brief_en: On August 11, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an executive order in the United States that significantly alters the childhood vaccination schedule. The order reduces the number of recommended vaccines from the 17 currently identified by the CDC to 11, including human papillomavirus (HPV) as a recommendation for all children. Key changes include the proposal to split the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate single-disease shots and the implementation of 'shared clinical decision-making' for several vaccines, which shifts the default to not vaccinating unless specifically requested by parents. Major medical bodies, such as the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, have criticized the order, arguing it lacks scientific evidence and could jeopardize public health by weakening confidence in immunization. While the order calls for improved research into vaccine timing and safety, medical experts maintain that the current schedule is supported by extensive scientific data.

news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 11 日,唐纳德·特朗普总统在美国签署了一项行政命令,显着改变了儿童 疫苗接种 时间表。该命令将推荐的 疫苗 数量从 CDC 目前确定的 17 种减少到 11 种,其中包括针对所有儿童的推荐 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV)。主要变化包括提议将麻疹、腮腺炎和风疹 (MMR) 疫苗 分成三种单独的单一疾病疫苗,以及对几种 疫苗 实施“共享临床决策”,这将默认情况改为不接种疫苗,除非父母特别要求。美国医学会和美国儿科学会等主要医疗机构批评了该命令,认为该命令缺乏科学证据,可能会削弱人们对免疫接种的信心,从而危及公众健康。虽然该命令要求改进对 疫苗 时间和安全性的研究,但医学专家坚持认为,当前的时间表得到了广泛的科学数据的支持。

news.content: Moe Alsumidaie Chief Editor Moe Alsumidaie is Chief Editor of The Clinical Trial Vanguard. Moe holds decades of experience in the clinical trials industry. Moe also serves as Head of Research at CliniBiz and Chief Data Scientist at Annex Clinical Corporation. Adaptive Clinical Trial Design Adaptive Trial Design Addiction Psychiatry AI in Clinical Trials alcohol use disorder Alzheimer's Disease Article Cell and Gene Therapy Clinical Operations Clinical Research Clinical Trial Design Clinical Trial Operations Clinical Trial Ops Brief Clinical Trial Quality Clinical Trials CLINOPS WATCHDOG CNS Trials Conference Coverage Decentralized Clinical Trials Digital Health Technologies dual diagnosis eClinical Tech News eClinical Technology EMA Executive Interviews FDA Enforcement FDA Guidance FDA Regulation FDA Regulatory Strategy FDA Warning Letter GCP Compliance GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Ketamine Therapy Oncology Trials Opinion Parkinson's Disease Pediatric Oncology Platform Trials Psychedelic Clinical Trials PSYCH PULSE Real-World Evidence site activation Site Operations study startup Treatment-Resistant Depression Search for:Search Button Articles Conference Coverage Executive Interviews News CliniCast News PDS Biotechnology Halts PDS0101 Trial, Pivots to PDS0301 in Colorectal Cancer By Jon Napitupulu August 12, 2026 PDS Biotechnology built its public identity around PDS0101, and a reported 39.3-month median overall survival in HPV16-positive first-line recurrent and metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma made that attachment understandable. Abandoning it anyway, as the company announced in an August 11 shareholder letter filed as an 8-K with the SEC, is the kind of move that demands explanation beyond routine pipeline pruning. The decision to halt internal investment in PDS0101, including the discontinuation of the Phase 3 VERSATILE-003 trial, signals that management concluded the capital required to run a confirmatory head and neck study could not be justified against what it sees as a more tractable opportunity elsewhere. That opportunity is PDS0301, a tumor-targeted IL-12 immunocytokine designed to remodel the tumor microenvironment, now repositioned as the company’s lead asset with metastatic colorectal cancer as the priority indication. The strategic logic is legible: IL-12 has long been recognized as a potent but toxicity-prone cytokine, and a tumor-targeted formulation attempts to confine activity to the lesion rather than flooding systemic circulation. Whether PDS0301 can deliver that profile at therapeutic doses in colorectal cancer is the clinical question the company is now betting its resources on. The pivot was disclosed simultaneously with the VERSATILE-003 halt, leaving no ambiguity about sequencing: this is a replacement, not a parallel track. The sacrifice of PDS0101 data is genuinely costly. The VERSATILE-002 Phase 2 result, a 39.3-month median overall survival in combination with pembrolizumab, was a credible signal in a setting where pembrolizumab is already an established standard of care. Stopping before Phase 3 readout means that number never matures into a label claim. For patients with HPV16-positive disease, that gap is real. For the company, the calculus was apparently that a fully resourced Phase 3 program in HNSCC, competing for attention against established pembrolizumab combination data, was less defensible than an earlier-stage bet in colorectal cancer where immunotherapy penetration remains a harder, but potentially more differentiated, problem. The single clinical marker to watch now is the dose-toxicity profile of PDS0301 in its colorectal studies. IL-12’s history of systemic inflammatory toxicity has ended promising programs before, and if PDS0301 cannot demonstrate clean tolerability at doses that produce meaningful tumor microenvironment remodeling, the logic of abandoning a 39.3-month survival asset collapses entirely. Adaptive Clinical Trial Design Adaptive Trial Design Addiction Psychiatry AI in Clinical Trials alcohol use disorder Alzheimer's Disease Article Cell and Gene Therapy Clinical Operations Clinical Research Clinical Trial Design Clinical Trial Operations Clinical Trial Ops Brief Clinical Trial Quality Clinical Trials CLINOPS WATCHDOG CNS Trials Conference Coverage Decentralized Clinical Trials Digital Health Technologies dual diagnosis eClinical Tech News eClinical Technology EMA Executive Interviews FDA Enforcement FDA Guidance FDA Regulation FDA Regulatory Strategy FDA Warning Letter GCP Compliance GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Ketamine Therapy Oncology Trials Opinion Parkinson's Disease Pediatric Oncology Platform Trials Psychedelic Clinical Trials PSYCH PULSE Real-World Evidence site activation Site Operations study startup Treatment-Resistant Depression Search for:Search Button Articles Conference Coverage Executive Interviews News CliniCast News PDS Biotechnology Halts PDS0101 Trial, Pivots to PDS0301 in Colorectal Cancer By Jon Napitupulu August 12, 2026 PDS Biotechnology built its public identity around PDS0101, and a reported 39.3-month median overall survival in HPV16-positive first-line recurrent and metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma made that attachment understandable. Abandoning it anyway, as the company announced in an August 11 shareholder letter filed as an 8-K with the SEC, is the kind of move that demands explanation beyond routine pipeline pruning. The decision to halt internal investment in PDS0101, including the discontinuation of the Phase 3 VERSATILE-003 trial, signals that management concluded the capital required to run a confirmatory head and neck study could not be justified against what it sees as a more tractable opportunity elsewhere. That opportunity is PDS0301, a tumor-targeted IL-12 immunocytokine designed to remodel the tumor microenvironment, now repositioned as the company’s lead asset with metastatic colorectal cancer as the priority indication. The strategic logic is legible: IL-12 has long been recognized as a potent but toxicity-prone cytokine, and a tumor-targeted formulation attempts to confine activity to the lesion rather than flooding systemic circulation. Whether PDS0301 can deliver that profile at therapeutic doses in colorectal cancer is the clinical question the company is now betting its resources on. The pivot was disclosed simultaneously with the VERSATILE-003 halt, leaving no ambiguity about sequencing: this is a replacement, not a parallel track. The sacrifice of PDS0101 data is genuinely costly. The VERSATILE-002 Phase 2 result, a 39.3-month median overall survival in combination with pembrolizumab, was a credible signal in a setting where pembrolizumab is already an established standard of care. Stopping before Phase 3 readout means that number never matures into a label claim. For patients with HPV16-positive disease, that gap is real. For the company, the calculus was apparently that a fully resourced Phase 3 program in HNSCC, competing for attention against established pembrolizumab combination data, was less defensible than an earlier-stage bet in colorectal cancer where immunotherapy penetration remains a harder, but potentially more differentiated, problem. The single clinical marker to watch now is the dose-toxicity profile of PDS0301 in its colorectal studies. IL-12’s history of systemic inflammatory toxicity has ended promising programs before, and if PDS0301 cannot demonstrate clean tolerability at doses that produce meaningful tumor microenvironment remodeling, the logic of abandoning a 39.3-month survival asset collapses entirely. analysis.time: The company announced the halt of the PDS0101 trial on August 11, 2026, and the decision was disclosed simultaneously with the VERSATILE-003 trial halt. The event date is August 11, 2026, with the publication date being August 12, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event involves PDS Biotechnology, a company based in the United States, and its clinical trials in the context of HPV16-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and metastatic colorectal cancer.
analysis.event: PDS Biotechnology halted its Phase 3 VERSATILE-003 trial for PDS0101 in HPV16-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and pivoted to PDS0301 for metastatic colorectal cancer. This decision was made based on strategic considerations regarding resource allocation and clinical potential.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The halt of the PDS0101 trial represents a significant shift in the company's research focus, with potential implications for patients who had been enrolled in the trial. The risk associated with this pivot lies in the unproven therapeutic potential of PDS0301 in colorectal cancer, particularly regarding its dose-toxicity profile and ability to achieve meaningful tumor microenvironment remodeling.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The company has halted the PDS0101 trial and pivoted to PDS0301, with no further details provided on the specific reasons for the decision. The response is based on internal strategic evaluation, and the outcome of the PDS0301 trials remains uncertain.

analysis.brief_en: PDS Biotechnology has halted its Phase 3 VERSATILE-003 trial for PDS0101, a treatment for HPV16-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, and shifted focus to PDS0301 for metastatic colorectal cancer. This decision, announced in an August 11 shareholder letter, reflects the company's strategic prioritization of resources toward a potentially more differentiated opportunity. The VERSATILE-002 Phase 2 trial had shown a 39.3-month median overall survival in combination with pembrolizumab, but stopping before Phase 3 means this data cannot mature into a label claim. The company now bets on PDS0301, an IL-12 immunocytokine designed to target tumors and reduce systemic toxicity. However, the success of PDS0301 depends on demonstrating clean tolerability at therapeutic doses, which remains uncertain. The pivot signals a shift in focus from HPV16-associated cancers to colorectal cancer, where immunotherapy penetration is still a challenge. The decision was disclosed simultaneously with the trial halt, leaving no ambiguity about the replacement strategy.

news.content_zh: PDS Biotechnology 已停止 PDS0101(一种治疗 HPV16 阳性头颈鳞状细胞癌的 治疗)的 3 期 VERSATILE-003 试验,并将重点转移到治疗转移性结直肠癌的 PDS0301。这一决定在 8 月 11 日的股东信中宣布,反映了公司对资源的战略优先顺序,以寻求潜在的更具差异化的机会。VERSATILE-002 2 期试验显示,与 pembrolizumab 联合使用,中位总生存期为 39.3 个月,但在 3 期之前停止意味着该数据无法成熟为标签声明。该公司现在押注于PDS0301,这是一种IL-12免疫细胞因子,旨在靶向肿瘤并减少全身毒性。然而,PDS0301 的成功取决于在治疗剂量下表现出完全的耐受性,这仍然不确定。这一枢纽标志着重点从 HPV16 相关癌症转向结直肠癌,而免疫疗法的渗透仍然是一个挑战。该决定是在试验停止的同时披露的,因此更换策略没有任何含糊之处。

news.content: You need to enable JavaScript to run this app. Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus German politicsUkraineHeat and drought Latest audioLatest videos Live TV Advertisement ScienceUnited States of America Making sense of Trump's executive order on US vaccinations Zulfikar Abbany 08/11/2026August 11, 2026 President Donald Trump and his Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long tried to reduce the number of vaccinations available to the US public and even farm animals. The latest move in context. https://p.dw.com/p/5Id3b Copy link The Trump Administration wants to separate the combined measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine into single shotsImage: Rebecca Blackwell/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement US President Donald Trump signed another executive order on Monday, August 10, 2026: "Delivering gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for Americans." The order reduces the current recommendation of 18 vaccines for children down to 11, which puts it almost in line with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations. As DW reported in May 2025, there are vaccines against 30 infectious diseases. The World Health Organization recommends that every child get vaccinated against 12 of those: Tuberculosis Hepatitis B Polio Diphtheria Tetanus Pertussis (whooping cough) Haemophilus influenza type B Pneumococcal disease Rotavirus Measles Rubella Human papillomavirus This is the WHO making recommendations for all nations — both rich and poor. Many poor countries face challenges around access to vaccines at prices they can afford and distributing them safely to people living in remote areas. Protecting vaccines in Ghana's rising heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 02:01 Rich countries, on the other hand, can afford and therefore usually offer more vaccinations than the WHO's base level of 12. But not all of them do. Germany, for example, recommends 14 vaccinations for children in their first two years after birth. Germany no longer recommends the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (TB), which is on the WHO list. It does recommend vaccination against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which is not on the WHO list. This just goes to show that there are variations around the world. It's not just the US. These variations often depend on which diseases are considered by local health experts to be an ongoing threat to any given community. Taking the example of TB in Germany: In 1998, the country's Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) decided the risk of TB infections was low, and herd immunity was deemed high enough at 50-80%. Therefore the STIKO stopped recommending the vaccine. Advertisement What does Trump's new childhood vaccine recommendation say? Trump wants to create three distinct categories for vaccination. The first category includes immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (meningitis), pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella (chickenpox). That removes vaccination against hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and RSV from this baseline category that were on the recommended list until now. These illnesses however can still affect newborns. As we reported in 2022, cases of RSV have risen in the US and Europe. Babies who don't receive the vaccine would remain unprotected against the illness. By contrast, Germany recommends vaccination for RSV, rotavirus and hepatitis B in a child's first six months. Trump's executive order also recommends that the combined MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella — which is a global standard — be split into individual jabs, spaced over time. This appears to be a reflection on long-held rhetoric from the Trump administration suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine causes autism. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says there is no published evidence to suggest there is any benefit in single jabs. In fact, its advice on the MMR vaccine states that "the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) agree that MMR vaccine is not responsible for recent increases in the number of children with autism." But Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long suggested vaccines are dangerous in general. Kennedy also thinks that the common painkiller Tylenol causes autism when taken during pregnancy. It is the only painkiller allowed during pregnancy in the US. And as we reported in September 2025, no high-quality scientific evidence substantiated their claim. Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 05:18 Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue. The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19. The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination. That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again. This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic. Allowing bird flu to spread Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle. Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well. On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance." Edited by: Carla Bleiker This article was updated on August 13, 2026, to correct an error in the original version. We had equated varicella virus with smallpox when it is in fact chickenpox. Kennedy Jr. have long tried to reduce the number of vaccinations available to the US public and even farm animals. The latest move in context. https://p.dw.com/p/5Id3b Copy link The Trump Administration wants to separate the combined measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine into single shotsImage: Rebecca Blackwell/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement US President Donald Trump signed another executive order on Monday, August 10, 2026: "Delivering gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for Americans." The order reduces the current recommendation of 18 vaccines for children down to 11, which puts it almost in line with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations. As DW reported in May 2025, there are vaccines against 30 infectious diseases. The World Health Organization recommends that every child get vaccinated against 12 of those: Tuberculosis Hepatitis B Polio Diphtheria Tetanus Pertussis (whooping cough) Haemophilus influenza type B Pneumococcal disease Rotavirus Measles Rubella Human papillomavirus This is the WHO making recommendations for all nations — both rich and poor. Many poor countries face challenges around access to vaccines at prices they can afford and distributing them safely to people living in remote areas. Protecting vaccines in Ghana's rising heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 02:01 Rich countries, on the other hand, can afford and therefore usually offer more vaccinations than the WHO's base level of 12. But not all of them do. Germany, for example, recommends 14 vaccinations for children in their first two years after birth. Germany no longer recommends the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis (TB), which is on the WHO list. It does recommend vaccination against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), which is not on the WHO list. This just goes to show that there are variations around the world. It's not just the US. These variations often depend on which diseases are considered by local health experts to be an ongoing threat to any given community. Taking the example of TB in Germany: In 1998, the country's Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) decided the risk of TB infections was low, and herd immunity was deemed high enough at 50-80%. Therefore the STIKO stopped recommending the vaccine. Advertisement What does Trump's new childhood vaccine recommendation say? Trump wants to create three distinct categories for vaccination. The first category includes immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b (meningitis), pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella (chickenpox). That removes vaccination against hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and RSV from this baseline category that were on the recommended list until now. These illnesses however can still affect newborns. As we reported in 2022, cases of RSV have risen in the US and Europe. Babies who don't receive the vaccine would remain unprotected against the illness. By contrast, Germany recommends vaccination for RSV, rotavirus and hepatitis B in a child's first six months. Trump's executive order also recommends that the combined MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella — which is a global standard — be split into individual jabs, spaced over time. This appears to be a reflection on long-held rhetoric from the Trump administration suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine causes autism. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says there is no published evidence to suggest there is any benefit in single jabs. In fact, its advice on the MMR vaccine states that "the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) agree that MMR vaccine is not responsible for recent increases in the number of children with autism." But Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have long suggested vaccines are dangerous in general. Kennedy also thinks that the common painkiller Tylenol causes autism when taken during pregnancy. It is the only painkiller allowed during pregnancy in the US. And as we reported in September 2025, no high-quality scientific evidence substantiated their claim. Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 05:18 Trump's second category would include immunizations for high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue. The third would include vaccines to be given "based on shared clinical decision-making" — so, doctor and patient or parent of a patient would have to agree. These include: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19. The effect of political — rather than scientific — rhetoric on vaccines While there's no direct recommendation to ban any vaccine, the second Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to destabilize public consensus over vaccination. That can cause confusion in the community and rising rates of infection. For example, in July 2026, DW reported how "amnesia" about measles and how dangerous it is had led to a rise in measles infections in the US. People had missed opportunities to get vaccinated because infection rates had been low, but then they rose again. This is not just the case in North America. Germany has also seen measles infections rise, with experts citing anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic. Allowing bird flu to spread Kennedy however takes his hands-off rhetoric to farming communities, too. In March 2025, DW reported how the health secretary suggested bird flu should be allowed to spread through bird populations, even in places where it had already infected cattle. Kennedy said it would enable researchers to develop "super" chickens. But instead, more than 150 million birds got infected. Bird flu virus was detected in raw milk. And there were bird-to-human infections as well. On Monday, when Trump's executive order was released, the AAP's Andrew Racine said it was "not based on 'gold-standard science.' There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance." Edited by: Carla Bleiker This article was updated on August 13, 2026, to correct an error in the original version. We had equated varicella virus with smallpox when it is in fact chickenpox. analysis.brief_en: On August 10, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order reducing the recommended number of childhood vaccines from 18 to 11 and reclassifying remaining vaccines into risk-based and shared-decision categories. The move, framed as aligning with World Health Organization recommendations, removes hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza, RSV, and varicella from the baseline schedule. The American Academy of Pediatrics criticized the order as lacking 'gold-standard science,' while the CDC has previously stated there is no evidence supporting the splitting of the MMR vaccine. Public health experts warn the policy could destabilize vaccination consensus, citing recent rises in measles infections in the U.S. and Europe linked to reduced vaccination rates and anti-vaccine rhetoric.

news.content: click Local News Sports Opinion NKY Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Q&A: Local health experts weigh in on child vaccines, new Trump guidelines Esther Launstein Cincinnati Enquirer Updated Aug. 11, 2026, 3:06 p.m. ET This story was updated because an earlier version included an inaccuracy. The Trump Administration recommends that state health agencies reduce the number of childhood vaccines and separate the doses of commonly combined immunizations, according to an executive order released Aug. 10. The order changes the recommended vaccines for all children and advises that commonly combined vaccinations, including the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine, be administered in three separate single-disease shots at separate medical appointments. But what do these recommendations mean for children in Ohio? The Enquirer spoke with Dr. Steve Feagins, the medical director at Hamilton County Public Health, and Dr. Chris Peltier, a board-certified pediatrician at Pediatric Associates of Mt. Carmel and previous president of the Ohio chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity. What are the current recommendations for childhood vaccinations? Feagins: The recommendations have not changed, nor has the law. The requirements for the 10 diseases that children are vaccinated against prior to entering kindergarten is Ohio State law. And so we, your local health department, follow the guidelines and the requirements of the Ohio Department of Health, which typically takes its guidelines from the CDC. Peltier: There is no new research or evidence that supports the executive order that was signed yesterday. We know from decades of research and thousands of studies that vaccines are safe. Vaccines work. They do not cause autism, and really the schedule that the American Academy of Pediatrics has put out has been well-studied and is based on evidence. Recommended vaccine schedule from the American Academy of Pediatrics: At birth: Hepatitis B; respiratory syncytial virus. 2 months old: Diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough (DTaP) combined vaccine; pneumococcal conjugate; Haemophilus influenzae tybe B; polio; and rotavirus. 1 year old: measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) combined; chicken pox / varicella; hepatitis A; COVID-19; and influenza. Teens: Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis (Tdap) combined vaccine; meningococcal meningitis; and human papillomavirus. Recommended changes from the Trump Administration: All children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella. High-risk populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue. What is the reasoning behind the Trump Administration's recommended changes to the vaccine schedule? Peltier: The rationale that we have heard, both from the Secretary (Robert F.) Kennedy (Jr.) and Health and Human Services as well as the president, is that they are trying to align our vaccine schedule closer to that of Denmark. Denmark does fewer vaccinations that we do in the United States. The problem is we don't live in Denmark. It's a different country, different population and obviously a much different size. They have a much different health system than we do. Denmark has opted to invest more money in reactive health care. So, if a child does get a vaccine preventable illness, their health system is much more equipped to take care of those kids. Whereas that's not the case in this country. So, our goal is to prevent illness because oftentimes we know that our health care systems are undermanned and Medicaid is being slashed. Funding is being cut, which really decreases the care that kids get once they get sick. You can't compare healthcare in Denmark to healthcare in the United States. It just doesn't make sense. How are vaccine schedules developed? Feagins: The various experts on adult vaccinations as well as childhood diseases come together in a prescribed fashion to develop the guidelines. And we've followed those from the Academy for decades, and they've very much been in line with the CDC guidelines historically. Peltier: Vaccinating kids against vaccine preventable illnesses obviously prevents those illnesses. One recommended change is giving measles, mumps and rubella as separate vaccines over several appointments. What would be the impact? Peltier: There was talk in the press conference yesterday about MMR causing fatal reactions. That is just not true. The evidence does not support that. There has never been a death due to the MMR vaccine. There is no science to back up splitting them up. We know the science supports giving a combined MMR vaccine at age 12 months and at age 4 years. It's safe. There really isn't any good science to support that recommendation. It really does a couple of things. It's only going to end up delaying vaccination rates, delaying getting kids completely vaccinated, and it's going to cause more disease because now families have to come to a physician's office three different times. Those have to be would have to be separated by at least a month because they're live virus vaccines, and you have to wait a month minimum in between administering those. The other thing is, there currently is no manufacturer that makes single measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. That would take time, an investment in capital, and I'm not sure there's really any incentive for a vaccine manufacturer to invest that kind of money to develop three new vaccines that we don't need. The Trump Administration also cited links between vaccines and autism as reasons for the changes. What does science show? Peltier: The science shows us that there is no link. There is study after study involving thousands of children that show no link between vaccines and autism. It just doesn't exist. Feagins: There have been large national and international studies comparing large numbers of children who received vaccinations and those who did not. And the incidence of autism remains the same. And so, we conclude from that that there does not appear to be a cause-and-effect relationship to vaccinations and subsequent development of autism. What advice would you give to parents about their vaccination options going into the schoolyear? Feagins: I don't know any parents who don't want the best for their children. I don't know any physicians or clinicians who don't want the best for their patients, and so the advice is have the conversation, talk with your trusted clinician and decide on what's the best course for you. As we enter the school year, we just wanted to point out that it's a good thing to get your vaccines get lined up. These vaccines are for a reason, so that you cannot just protect your child but all children, including those who may not be vaccinated. Peltier: It's completely natural to have questions when you're a parent. You want to do what's best and safe for your kids. So my best advice would be talk to your pediatrician, ask them questions about vaccines so that we can share with you why we do what we do, why we follow the American Academy of Pediatric schedule.
