news.content_original: click Local News Sports Opinion NKY Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Q&A: Local health experts weigh in on child vaccines, new Trump guidelines Esther Launstein Cincinnati Enquirer Updated Aug. 11, 2026, 3:06 p.m. ET This story was updated because an earlier version included an inaccuracy. The Trump Administration recommends that state health agencies reduce the number of childhood vaccines and separate the doses of commonly combined immunizations, according to an executive order released Aug. 10. The order changes the recommended vaccines for all children and advises that commonly combined vaccinations, including the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine, be administered in three separate single-disease shots at separate medical appointments. But what do these recommendations mean for children in Ohio? The Enquirer spoke with Dr. Steve Feagins, the medical director at Hamilton County Public Health, and Dr. Chris Peltier, a board-certified pediatrician at Pediatric Associates of Mt. Carmel and previous president of the Ohio chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity. What are the current recommendations for childhood vaccinations? Feagins: The recommendations have not changed, nor has the law. The requirements for the 10 diseases that children are vaccinated against prior to entering kindergarten is Ohio State law. And so we, your local health department, follow the guidelines and the requirements of the Ohio Department of Health, which typically takes its guidelines from the CDC. Peltier: There is no new research or evidence that supports the executive order that was signed yesterday. We know from decades of research and thousands of studies that vaccines are safe. Vaccines work. They do not cause autism, and really the schedule that the American Academy of Pediatrics has put out has been well-studied and is based on evidence. Recommended vaccine schedule from the American Academy of Pediatrics: At birth: Hepatitis B; respiratory syncytial virus. 2 months old: Diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough (DTaP) combined vaccine; pneumococcal conjugate; Haemophilus influenzae tybe B; polio; and rotavirus. 1 year old: measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) combined; chicken pox / varicella; hepatitis A; COVID-19; and influenza. Teens: Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis (Tdap) combined vaccine; meningococcal meningitis; and human papillomavirus. Recommended changes from the Trump Administration: All children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella. High-risk populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue. What is the reasoning behind the Trump Administration's recommended changes to the vaccine schedule? Peltier: The rationale that we have heard, both from the Secretary (Robert F.) Kennedy (Jr.) and Health and Human Services as well as the president, is that they are trying to align our vaccine schedule closer to that of Denmark. Denmark does fewer vaccinations that we do in the United States. The problem is we don't live in Denmark. It's a different country, different population and obviously a much different size. They have a much different health system than we do. Denmark has opted to invest more money in reactive health care. So, if a child does get a vaccine preventable illness, their health system is much more equipped to take care of those kids. Whereas that's not the case in this country. So, our goal is to prevent illness because oftentimes we know that our health care systems are undermanned and Medicaid is being slashed. Funding is being cut, which really decreases the care that kids get once they get sick. You can't compare healthcare in Denmark to healthcare in the United States. It just doesn't make sense. How are vaccine schedules developed? Feagins: The various experts on adult vaccinations as well as childhood diseases come together in a prescribed fashion to develop the guidelines. And we've followed those from the Academy for decades, and they've very much been in line with the CDC guidelines historically. Peltier: Vaccinating kids against vaccine preventable illnesses obviously prevents those illnesses. One recommended change is giving measles, mumps and rubella as separate vaccines over several appointments. What would be the impact? Peltier: There was talk in the press conference yesterday about MMR causing fatal reactions. That is just not true. The evidence does not support that. There has never been a death due to the MMR vaccine. There is no science to back up splitting them up. We know the science supports giving a combined MMR vaccine at age 12 months and at age 4 years. It's safe. There really isn't any good science to support that recommendation. It really does a couple of things. It's only going to end up delaying vaccination rates, delaying getting kids completely vaccinated, and it's going to cause more disease because now families have to come to a physician's office three different times. Those have to be would have to be separated by at least a month because they're live virus vaccines, and you have to wait a month minimum in between administering those. The other thing is, there currently is no manufacturer that makes single measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. That would take time, an investment in capital, and I'm not sure there's really any incentive for a vaccine manufacturer to invest that kind of money to develop three new vaccines that we don't need. The Trump Administration also cited links between vaccines and autism as reasons for the changes. What does science show? Peltier: The science shows us that there is no link. There is study after study involving thousands of children that show no link between vaccines and autism. It just doesn't exist. Feagins: There have been large national and international studies comparing large numbers of children who received vaccinations and those who did not. And the incidence of autism remains the same. And so, we conclude from that that there does not appear to be a cause-and-effect relationship to vaccinations and subsequent development of autism. What advice would you give to parents about their vaccination options going into the schoolyear? Feagins: I don't know any parents who don't want the best for their children. I don't know any physicians or clinicians who don't want the best for their patients, and so the advice is have the conversation, talk with your trusted clinician and decide on what's the best course for you. As we enter the school year, we just wanted to point out that it's a good thing to get your vaccines get lined up. These vaccines are for a reason, so that you cannot just protect your child but all children, including those who may not be vaccinated. Peltier: It's completely natural to have questions when you're a parent. You want to do what's best and safe for your kids. So my best advice would be talk to your pediatrician, ask them questions about vaccines so that we can share with you why we do what we do, why we follow the American Academy of Pediatric schedule. District magistrate Jitendra Pratap Singh, who reached the Urban Primary Health Centre in Rawatpur on Sunday to inspect the vaccination work and appealed to parents to get their eligible daughters vaccinated. So far, 18,377 adolescent girls in the district have been administered the HPV vaccine.The DM said that infection with the Human Papilloma Virus is a major cause of cervical cancer. The HPV vaccine is a safe and effective means of reducing the risk of this cancer in the future. Along with HPV vaccination for the prevention of cervical cancer, timely screening at the prescribed age is also important. This vaccine, which is expensive in private hospitals, is being made available completely free of cost to eligible adolescent girls by the government.He appealed to parents not to fall for any confusion, hesitation or rumours and to take their daughters to the vaccination centre. .
